Machine learning quantum data to accelerate quantum Monte Carlo

Tong Jiang Thanks: These authors contributed equally. Affiliation: Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA    Andrew Zhao Thanks: These authors contributed equally. Affiliation: Quantum Algorithms and Applications Collaboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Livermore, CA 94550, USA    Shashwat Kumar Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Santa Barbara, CA 93111, USA    Jigyasa Nigam Affiliation: Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA    Eliott Rosenberg Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Santa Barbara, CA 93111, USA    Ryan Babbush Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Santa Barbara, CA 93111, USA    Andrew D. Baczewski Affiliation: Quantum Algorithms and Applications Collaboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM 87185, USA    William J. Huggins Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Santa Barbara, CA 93111, USA    Joonho Lee Email: joonholee@g.harvard.edu Affiliation: Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Santa Barbara, CA 93111, USA
November 17, 2026
Abstract

Simulating strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials remains a central goal for quantum computing. A promising strategy uses quantum processors to prepare trial wavefunctions that guide classical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, the enormous computational cost of repeatedly processing quantum measurements has severely limited the practical scalability of this approach. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by compressing quantum measurement data into machine-learning models that efficiently provide the wavefunction overlaps needed by QMC. This accelerates quantum-classical QMC by orders of magnitude, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations with comparable accuracy. We demonstrate our approach on hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron–sulfur clusters using measurements from Google’s Willow processor. By enabling efficient reuse of quantum-state information on the classical coprocessor, our framework addresses a fundamental bottleneck in hybrid quantum algorithms that will persist even into the fault-tolerant era.

Introduction. Accurately simulating correlated electrons remains a central challenge in computational science, with applications ranging from molecular discovery to high-temperature superconductivity. 50, 22 Quantum computers offer a fundamentally different way to represent electronic correlation, motivating extensive efforts to develop quantum algorithms for chemistry and materials science. 2, 14, 6, 65 Among these approaches, quantum–classical hybrid quantum Monte Carlo (QC-QMC) has emerged as a promising strategy for achieving high accuracy. 30 In QC-QMC, a quantum processor prepares a correlated trial wavefunction whose overlaps with sampled many-body configurations (walkers) guide the classical Monte Carlo projection and help control the fermionic sign problem. The key promise of QC-QMC is that expressive quantum circuits can provide trial wavefunctions beyond the reach of classical approximations, while the subsequent Monte Carlo projection relaxes the accuracy requirements on quantum state preparation. Realizing this promise, however, requires an efficient interface between quantum overlap evaluations and classical QMC calculations.

To avoid the latency of repeated quantum–classical feedback, QC-QMC collects a reusable ensemble of randomized measurements of the trial state, from which a classical coprocessor estimates the overlaps required by QMC. 28, 30, 79, 71 Yet, repeatedly reconstructing these overlaps for the many walkers encountered throughout QMC propagation incurs enormous classical computational cost 38, 27. This postprocessing bottleneck has severely limited hardware demonstrations, which have so far reached only 16 qubits 30, 80, 51 and consumed over 13,000 GPU hours for a single calculation 80. Meanwhile, a 40-qubit calculation was estimated to require millions of CPU hours 51.

Here, we overcome this bottleneck by developing a machine learning (ML) framework (Fig. 1) that compresses quantum measurement data into a classical surrogate. 10, 15, 24, 56, 72, 29 Rather than reconstructing the full quantum state, we learn its overlaps with the many-body configurations relevant to QMC. Once trained, the surrogate efficiently supplies these overlaps and their derivatives, bypassing repeated classical postprocessing of quantum measurements. This reduces the computational cost by orders of magnitude and makes end-to-end QC-QMC on 40 qubits of Google’s Willow processor affordable, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations. At this scale, QC-QMC gives energies within chemical accuracy, for hydrogen chains with a mean-field trial and for an iron–sulfur cluster with a correlated trial.

Theory and algorithms. In projector QMC, the exact ground state, |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle, is obtained by imaginary-time propagation, which is approximated by a stochastically sampled ensemble of wavefunctions,

|Ψ0⟩∝limτ→∞e−τ​H^​|Φ0⟩,|Ψ⁡(τ)⟩≈∑i=1Nwwi​|ϕi⟩.|\Psi_{0}\rangle\propto\lim_{\tau\rightarrow\infty}e^{-\tau\hat{H}}|\Phi_{0}\rangle,\qquad|\Psi(\tau)\rangle\approx\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{w}}}w_{i}|\phi_{i}\rangle. (1)

The initial state |Φ0⟩|\Phi_{0}\rangle is assumed to have nonzero overlap with the ground state, and {|ϕi⟩}\{|\phi_{i}\rangle\} are statistical sample wavefunctions, known as walkers, with associated weights {wi}\{w_{i}\}. In unconstrained QMC, cancellations among walker weights cause the signal-to-noise ratio to decay exponentially with increasing imaginary time and system size, a manifestation of the notorious fermionic sign problem 76. Practical QMC methods control this instability by guiding the calculation with constraints imposed by a trial wavefunction |ΨT⟩|\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}\rangle. In this work, we use auxiliary-field QMC, 77, 49 but our technique is applicable to other QMC methods 35, 7. The trial wavefunction enters QMC through its overlaps with the walkers, ⟨ΨT|ϕi⟩\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}|\phi_{i}\rangle, and their derivatives, which determine the walker evolution and energy estimates (Supplementary Sec. S2.1).

To obtain these overlaps from a quantum-prepared trial state 30, we perform randomized measurements via Clifford matchgate circuits, yielding classical snapshots that we store and reuse to estimate overlaps with the walkers 71. Using an improved algorithm for processing matchgate shadows, we can process each snapshot per overlap with 𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}) cost, where NN is the number of qubits (Supplementary Sec. S4). This operation must be repeated for NsN_{\mathrm{s}} measurements, NwN_{\mathrm{w}} walkers, and NτN_{\tau} imaginary-time steps, resulting in a cost of 𝒪⁡(N3​Ns​Nw​Nτ)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}N_{\mathrm{s}}N_{\mathrm{w}}N_{\tau}) for the overlaps alone, before accounting for the derivatives needed for the importance sampling and energy estimates.

Our central idea is to decouple quantum-measurement processing from repeated overlap evaluations during QMC. We first estimate complex-valued overlaps for a much smaller set of Ntrain≪Nw​NτN_{\mathrm{train}}\ll N_{\mathrm{w}}N_{\tau} training determinants and use them to train a differentiable surrogate overlap model fθ​(ϕ)∝⟨ΨT|ϕ⟩f_{\theta}(\phi)\propto\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}|\phi\rangle. This introduces a one-time labeling cost of 𝒪⁡(N3​Ns​Ntrain)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}N_{\mathrm{s}}N_{\mathrm{train}}). Subsequent QMC propagation queries only the trained surrogate, whose evaluation cost is independent of NsN_{\mathrm{s}} and whose derivatives can be evaluated directly without reprocessing the quantum measurements. Further details are provided in Supplementary Sec. S2.

In principle, the surrogate can be any differentiable model of the overlap trained on the measurement data. We train fθf_{\theta} by supervised learning on overlap labels representative of those used by QMC. Because the training labels are obtained from noisy quantum measurements, care must be taken to prevent the model from fitting overlap uncertainty due to the measurement noise and a finite number of measurements 64, 11, 44. We quantify the relative statistical error of the experimental labels by a noise floor FF, estimated from fluctuations across subsets of the measurement circuits (Supplementary Sec. S2.2 and Fig. S2.2). Since the labels have an uncertainty level on the order of FF itself, a learned model whose relative error on the validation labels (Eq. (S2.17)) falls below FF may be fitting uncertainty. We therefore use this as a stopping criterion for the training.

In general, the quantum trial states may be prepared through variational quantum algorithms 12, high-fidelity quantum state preparation 5, or quantum implementations of sophisticated classical wavefunctions. We demonstrate our ML-surrogate framework in two settings. First, we use mean-field trial wavefunctions for hydrogen chains containing up to 20 atoms (H20\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{20}}}, 40 qubits) to benchmark our proposed approach. To enable ML inference for arbitrary QMC walker configurations, we extend neural quantum states (NQS) 10 to accept arbitrary Slater determinants as inputs. Training NQS with randomized quantum measurements has shown promise 29, 72, but previous models were restricted to bit-string amplitudes, rather than the overlaps with rotated Slater determinants required by auxiliary-field QMC.

Second, for strongly correlated iron–sulfur complexes, preparing an accurate trial wavefunction directly on near-term quantum hardware remains prohibitively expensive. For our hardware demonstration, we instead assume access to an accurate wavefunction and approximate it with shallow quantum circuits, whose parameters we optimize classically to reproduce overlaps with representative training walkers. We then execute these circuits on quantum hardware, collect randomized measurements, and train our ML surrogate based on nonorthogonal configuration interaction (NOCI) 36, 18. This enables chemically accurate QC-QMC calculations for [Fe2S2(SCH3)4]2- in 28- and 40-qubit active spaces, despite hardware noise.

Results and discussion. The experiments in this work were performed on a Google Willow quantum processor 21, which has over a hundred qubits, two-qubit gate error rates on the order of 10−310^{-3} (Supplementary Fig. S1.1), and reported repetition rates of approximately 6×1046\times 10^{4} shots per second. This enables us to collect millions of classical shadow measurements every few minutes. To suppress the effects of hardware noise, we employ randomized compiling, dynamical decoupling, parity postselection, and qubit-assignment averaging (Supplementary Sec. S1.2).

Hydrogen chains are a standard benchmark for strongly correlated electronic structure methods 46, 47, as the degree of electronic correlation can be tuned by varying the interatomic separation. Increasing the chain length also provides a systematic way to assess how computational methods scale with system size. As a controlled benchmark of our ML framework, we use a spin-unrestricted Hartree–Fock (HF) trial state for hydrogen chains up to H20\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{20}}}, performing the experiments and QMC calculations in the HF basis. We show the circuit in Fig. 2a: a GHZ-type state is prepared, and each spin register is then measured through its own random Clifford matchgate circuit. Measuring the two registers separately suffices because each QMC walker is a product of an α\alpha and a β\beta determinant 78 (Supplementary Sec. S5.2). Together with an improved compilation (Supplementary Sec. S5.1), this keeps the circuit sizes compact (Supplementary Fig. S1.2). At every size, our matchgate circuits need under a third of the CZ\mathrm{CZ} gates and under half the depth of the full matchgate circuits used in previous experiments 80. Shallower circuits accumulate less hardware noise per snapshot, which is crucial for extracting useful overlap information (Supplementary Fig. S3.4).

We train an expressive NQS surrogate directly on noisy measurement data, starting from a random initialization with no classical initial guess. Fig. 2b shows the QC-QMC energies obtained with the trained surrogate as the QMC trial, relative to the ideal limit (infinite number of shots and noiseless devices) of QMC with HF trial. At every size, the deviation averaged over networks trained with different random seeds (Fig. S3.6) lies within chemical accuracy (1 kcal mol-1). Fig. 2c compares the cost of our approach with that of conventional QC-QMC, which evaluates every overlap, force bias, and local energy directly from the snapshots, using our optimized GPU implementation (Supplementary Fig. S2.1). At 8 and 16 qubits, conventional QC-QMC needs 100 and 2,500 circuits, respectively, at 500 shots each, to reach chemical accuracy. With the same data, our ML model reduces QC-QMC cost by 190-fold (8 qubits) and 4,100-fold (16 qubits). This comparison includes the cost of labeling the training data, training the NQS model, and running QMC end-to-end (Table S3.1). At 24 qubits and beyond, the estimated cost of processing all measurement data using conventional QC-QMC exceeds 10510^{5} GPU hours, making direct benchmarking prohibitively expensive. At these sizes, the one-time cost of producing the training labels dominates the total cost of our ML approach (>90%), which is still orders of magnitude smaller than a conventional QC-QMC run.

We next turn to a widely studied strongly correlated system: the iron–sulfur cluster. This class of transition-metal complexes facilitates electron transfer and catalysis across a wide range of biological processes 3. Their electronic structure is challenging owing to competing spin couplings among iron dd electrons, which produce many nearly degenerate spin states 61, 42, 75, 57, and charge fluctuations between iron and sulfur atoms. Achieving high accuracy at low computational cost for this compound and related systems has been challenging for both classical QMC 39 and near-term quantum methods such as sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) 59, 58, 16, 37. This provides a more demanding test of our framework than the hydrogen chain benchmark.

For this demonstration, we use a shallow, hardware-efficient ansatz based on the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) 30, 48, as in the SQD study 59 but with a different parameterization (Supplementary Sec. S1.3). We optimize the LUCJ circuit parameters to reproduce overlaps between the reference wavefunction and training walkers. Interestingly, direct variational energy minimization of the LUCJ wavefunction does not yield accurate QC-QMC results (Table S1.3). Here, we use a compact NOCI expansion 36, 18 as the surrogate, initialized from an inexpensive classical calculation and subsequently trained on quantum measurements. This provides a direct comparison with a classically optimized NOCI trial containing the same number of determinants, allowing us to assess the benefit of learning from quantum data. We study two active spaces, (18-electron, 14-orbital) and (30-electron, 20-orbital), hereafter denoted as (18e, 14o) and (30e, 20o), respectively, which map onto 28 and 40 qubits.

In Fig. 3a, we show the quantum circuit for (18e, 14o): a GHZ-type preparation followed by a shallow LUCJ ansatz, measured with spin-blocked randomized measurements 78 (matchgate shadows). Each spin register runs along a two-row snake on Willow (Fig. 3b). The spin-coupled circuit places its α\alpha–β\beta Jastrow pairs on the couplers (light orange) between the two snakes, whereas the spin-uncoupled circuit omits them and runs as two independent 15-qubit circuits including ancillas.

Fig. 3c compares classical QMC and QC-QMC for the singlet ground state. To illustrate the difficulty of this problem, we show the coupled-cluster (CC) hierarchy up to singles (S), doubles (D), triples (T), and quadruples (Q), where the trial energy improves as one adds more excitations, but the QMC error does not quickly converge to chemical accuracy. 39 Even CCSDTQ, whose own energy is within chemical accuracy, leaves an AFQMC error of 2.8 kcal mol-1 when its linearized wavefunction is used as the trial. In contrast, our quantum trial achieves chemical accuracy on Willow both with and without the α\alpha–β\beta Jastrow couplings, with errors of −0.86​(6)-0.86(6) and −0.85​(11)-0.85(11) kcal mol-1, respectively (Supplementary Fig. S3.8). This experiment collected 1.3×1081.3\times 10^{8} and 2.5×1072.5\times 10^{7} postselected snapshots for the spin-coupled and -uncoupled circuits, respectively (Supplementary Table S1.1). By contrast, a classical NOCI trial with the same number of determinants (four) as our spin-coupled surrogate, optimized for its variational energy, has a lower variational energy than our quantum trials yet yields an AFQMC energy about 5 kcal mol-1 below the exact result, and classical NOCI trials with 2–8 determinants all miss chemical accuracy (Supplementary Fig. S3.7). This highlights the role of quantum data in generating an accurate QMC trial wavefunction.

In Fig. 3d, we calculate the energy gap between the singlet and the S=5S=5 high-spin state. CC methods systematically improve and approach the exact value at CCSDTQ. QC-QMC, with both spin states guided by the measurement-trained trial surrogate, gives 20.2(1) kcal mol-1 against the exact 19.3 kcal mol-1, within chemical accuracy and on par with CCSDTQ. Our experimental QC-QMC closely reproduces the ideal (noiseless, infinite-shot) QC-QMC results, highlighting the noise robustness of QC-QMC combined with the ML surrogate. Notably, the spin-uncoupled trial is as accurate as the spin-coupled one, so the α\alpha–β\beta Jastrow pairs are not needed here. Without explicit opposite-spin Jastrow couplings in the trial, the circuit has no gates between the spin registers and splits into two independent halves, enabling experiments with reduced circuit complexity. For S=5S=5, the α\alpha-spin sector is fully occupied, so a nontrivial α\alpha-spin circuit is unnecessary (Supplementary Sec. S3.6).

Finally, we use the spin-uncoupled trial wavefunction for the (30e, 20o) active space, corresponding to a 40-qubit total system run as two 21-qubit circuits (Fig. 4). Using 3.0×1083.0\times 10^{8} postselected snapshots and a NOCI surrogate, QC-QMC achieves chemical accuracy for the singlet ground state (0.91​(8)0.91(8) kcal mol-1) relative to the exact energy. Unlike the singlet, where nearest-neighbor Jastrow pairs suffice, the S=5S=5 state requires pairs beyond nearest neighbors. Routing these pairs along the qubit line makes the circuit too deep to run at sufficiently high fidelity on the current device, so we classically emulate the quantum data using fast quantum circuit simulators 31. We train an ML model on these emulated data as we do for the experimental data (Supplementary Table S1.1 and Fig. S2.2c). Combining the experimental singlet results with the simulated high-spin data yields the spin gap within chemical accuracy.

Conclusions and outlook. Our work overcomes a major computational bottleneck in hybrid quantum–classical computing by compressing quantum measurement data into reusable machine-learning models. This accelerates QC-QMC by orders of magnitude, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations. Because the classical postprocessing bottleneck persists even on fault-tolerant quantum computers, our approach addresses a fundamental challenge for both near-term and future quantum computing.

A remaining challenge is the statistical measurement cost of resolving overlaps that decay exponentially with system size 43, 40. Although this limitation has not prevented our present calculations, even for strongly correlated systems such as iron–sulfur clusters, understanding its impact at larger scales will be crucial for identifying problems where QC-QMC can achieve practical quantum advantage. More broadly, our results establish a pathway toward scalable hybrid algorithms in which quantum information can be efficiently exploited by classical many-body methods.
