S1 Quantum-state preparation and measurements

S1.1 Hardware implementation

Qubit layouts and error rates.

Figure S1.1 shows the qubit layouts used on the Willow processor for the 40-qubit hydrogen chain and for [Fe2S2(SCH3)4]2- in (18e, 14o) and (30e, 20o), together with their single-qubit, two-qubit (CZ) and readout error rates. Single-qubit and readout errors are similar for the three layouts. CZ errors are lower for the hydrogen chain than for the two [Fe2S2(SCH3)4]2- layouts, since a one-dimensional path can avoid poor couplers more easily than a compact two-dimensional grid.

Circuits, gate counts, and shots.

Each hardware circuit consists of a GHZ-type preparation, the trial circuit, and a random matchgate circuit for the shadow measurement. Each spin sector of NN orbitals is mapped by the Jordan–Wigner transformation onto a line of NN qubits. When a sector has an odd number of electrons in the trial, we prepend one ancilla mode, so both physical registers have even fermion parity. This is essential for the matchgate shadows overlap formula 71. Initialized in a GHZ-type state, each circuit prepares (|𝟎⟩+|ΨT⟩)/2(|\mathbf{0}\rangle+|\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}\rangle)/\sqrt{2} due to particle-number symmetry. For the hydrogen chain experiments, |ΨT⟩=|1N/2,0N/2⟩α⊗|1N/2,0N/2⟩β|\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}\rangle=|1^{N/2},0^{N/2}\rangle_{\alpha}\otimes|1^{N/2},0^{N/2}\rangle_{\beta}. We map this to a one-dimensional line of 2​N2N qubits by ordering the spin sectors head-to-head, i.e., orbital indices ascending from the middle of the line outwards.

For the hydrogen chains, only the GHZ-type preparation and measurement circuit run on the device; for [Fe2S2(SCH3)4]2-, we insert a single-layer LUCJ ansatz between the GHZ preparation and measurement. Here we record the gate and shot counts for each circuit. In Table S1.1 we give a breakdown of the two-qubit (CZ) gates in each circuit, according to the GHZ-type preparation, the LUCJ ansatz (if applicable), and the Clifford matchgate measurements (on average over 100 random circuits). In Fig. S1.2 we display the matchgate circuit sizes in terms of both gates and depth. In particular, we compare them with full (non-spin-blocked) matchgates considered in previous experiments. We display an example of a spin-blocked matchgate circuit diagram in Fig. S1.3, and of the LUCJ circuits in Figs. S1.5 and S1.6.

S1.2 Error mitigation

Our experiments use relatively few algorithmic quantum error mitigation strategies. Here we describe the circuit-level error mitigation techniques used in this work.

Overlap ratios with shadows.

By and large, the most significant contribution to mitigating errors in QC-QMC is the inherent twirling of noise channels by classical shadows 13. For global Clifford shadows, this manifests as an overall scale factor that is uniform over all traceless observables. Since AFQMC only requires overlap ratios, this scale factor ideally cancels; this phenomenon was precisely observed in the original QC-QMC demonstration 30. Note that exact cancellation requires certain assumptions on the device noise (namely, Markovian and gate-independent) which are not obeyed in practice. The deviation in the presence of gate-dependent noise has been studied previously 78, 9. The previous discussion concerns global Clifford shadows; for matchgate shadows, the noise twirl does not yield just two irreps, but rather n+1n+1 irreps 78. The cancellation of errors due to taking overlap ratios using matchgate shadows was studied by Huang et al 27. They observed that despite the more delicate nature of the irreps of the matchgate group, a cancellation still persists under the same Markovian, gate-independent assumptions. We observe the same phenomenon in our experiments; Fig. S1.4 plots a sample of the training overlaps for the 40-qubit UHF data. The noisy overlaps show clear attenuation, which we can approximately correct by taking ratios. Note that these are overlaps computed directly from the shadows, before any ML training.

Qubit error suppression.

We utilize randomized compiling (RC) 70 and dynamical decoupling (DD) 68 for each random circuit that we run. RC involves inserting random single-qubit Clifford gates around each two-qubit gate such that the modified circuit is equivalent to the original circuit in the noiseless limit. In the presence of device noise, RC primarily converts coherent errors into incoherent errors, whose effects are easier to manage. This is especially amenable to the inherent noise twirling of classical shadows 13. DD involves a sequence of XX and YY gates whenever a qubit idles during circuit layers, with the effect being identity without noise. In the presence of errors, DD suppresses T2T_{2} dephasing by toggling the qubit’s frame while it idles. Note that due to the dramatic difference in rates of repeating a single circuit NN times vs. changing NN different circuits, it is infeasible to compile a new RC and DD sequence for each shot per circuit. Thus the sequences are fixed over all shots of the same circuit.

Parity postselection.

Because each trial has an even electron number (enforced in some cases by appending dummy qubits), and because we specifically choose every matchgate to preserve parity, the parity of every circuit output

UQ​(|𝟎⟩+|ΨT⟩2),det(Q)=1,U_{Q}\mathopen{}\left(\frac{|\mathbf{0}\rangle+|\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\mathclose{},\qquad\det(Q)=1, (S1.1)

is even in the absence of noise. Note that particle number itself is not generally preserved by the matchgates, so we can only postselect on parity. However, with spin-blocked matchgate shadows, we have a further symmetry that the parity in each spin sector is even; this is what we postselect on. Some representative postselection rates are displayed in Table S1.2. Section S3.3 discusses its effect on the overlap estimates, shown in Fig. S3.4.

Qubit assignment averaging.

Finally, we apply qubit assignment averaging (QAA), as in previous experiments 20. This involves rotating/flipping the assignment of simulated spin orbitals to physical qubits on the chip across the many measurements collected during the experiment. This reduces anisotropic error-rate effects across the chip that bias certain observables. This improves the inherent noise resilience of classical shadows, due to the noise-twirling property, in classical simulations of noise models 78. For the hydrogen chains, where the physical qubit layout is also a one-dimensional chain, there are only two assignments: if 1​α,2​α,…1\alpha,2\alpha,\ldots denote the canonical ordering of α\alpha spin orbitals, and similarly 1​β,2​β,…1\beta,2\beta,\ldots, then the two variants are (let NN be the number of molecular orbitals)

N​α,…,1​α,1​β,…,N​β,\displaystyle N\alpha,\ldots,1\alpha,1\beta,\ldots,N\beta, (S1.2)
N​β,…,1​β,1​α,…,N​α.\displaystyle N\beta,\ldots,1\beta,1\alpha,\ldots,N\alpha. (S1.3)

For LUCJ circuits, we can flip lengthwise and switch which block is α\alpha or β\beta. That is, we have the four assignments (0​α,0​β0\alpha,0\beta denote the ancilla orbitals):

0​α,1​α,…,N​α0​β,1​β,…,N​βN​α,…,1​α,0​αN​β,…,1​β,0​β0​β,1​β,…,N​β0​α,1​α,…,N​αN​β,…,1​β,0​βN​α,…,1​α,0​α\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{c|c}\begin{aligned} &0\alpha,1\alpha,\ldots,N\alpha\\ &0\beta,1\beta,\ldots,N\beta\end{aligned}&\begin{aligned} &N\alpha,\ldots,1\alpha,0\alpha\\ &N\beta,\ldots,1\beta,0\beta\end{aligned}\\ \hline\cr\begin{aligned} &0\beta,1\beta,\ldots,N\beta\\ &0\alpha,1\alpha,\ldots,N\alpha\end{aligned}&\begin{aligned} &N\beta,\ldots,1\beta,0\beta\\ &N\alpha,\ldots,1\alpha,0\alpha\end{aligned}\end{array}

All four are used for the (28+2)(28+2)-qubit LUCJ circuit; for the (40+2)(40+2)-qubit circuit, because of a minor hardware constraint, we could not flip the qubit assignment left to right, so we only used the two assignments that swap between α\alpha and β\beta registers.

S1.3 Local unitary cluster Jastrow ansatz

We follow the circuit structure of the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) ansatz 30, 48. We use the geometry of two adjacent snaked qubit chains (one for each spin type) embedded into the two-dimensional square lattice geometry of the Willow chip; see Figs. 3 and 4 in the main text (see also Fig. S1.1) for the exact arrangement.

We use a single LUCJ layer with a final orbital rotation, acting on the broken-symmetry unrestricted Hartree–Fock (BS-UHF) determinant |Φ0⟩|\Phi_{0}\rangle,

|ΨLUCJ⟩=eKf​eK​ei​J​e−K​|Φ0⟩,|\Psi_{\mathrm{LUCJ}}\rangle=e^{K_{\mathrm{f}}}\,e^{K}e^{iJ}e^{-K}|\Phi_{0}\rangle, (S1.6)

with

K=∑σ∑p​qκp​qσ​ap​σ†​aq​σ,Kf=∑σ∑p​qκp​qf,σ​ap​σ†​aq​σ,J=∑σ​τ∑(p,q)∈ℳσ​τJp​qσ​τ​np​σ​nq​τ,K=\sum_{\sigma}\sum_{pq}\kappa^{\sigma}_{pq}\,a_{p\sigma}^{\dagger}a_{q\sigma},\qquad K_{\mathrm{f}}=\sum_{\sigma}\sum_{pq}\kappa^{\mathrm{f},\sigma}_{pq}\,a_{p\sigma}^{\dagger}a_{q\sigma},\qquad J=\sum_{\sigma\tau}\sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal{M}_{\sigma\tau}}J^{\sigma\tau}_{pq}\,n_{p\sigma}n_{q\tau}, (S1.7)

where κσ\kappa^{\sigma} and κf,σ\kappa^{\mathrm{f},\sigma} are general anti-Hermitian matrices and Jp​qσ​τJ^{\sigma\tau}_{pq} are real. The orbital rotations are independent for the two spins (κα≠κβ\kappa^{\alpha}\neq\kappa^{\beta}): the reference is a broken-symmetry determinant whose α\alpha and β\beta orbitals differ, and the rotations of each spin are written in that spin’s BS-UHF molecular-orbital basis, so that setting all parameters to zero returns |Φ0⟩|\Phi_{0}\rangle. The interaction mask ℳ\mathcal{M} follows the qubit connectivity. The same-spin terms couple nearest neighbors along each chain, (p,p+1)(p,p+1). The spin-coupled circuit adds opposite-spin on-site terms (p,p)(p,p) at the sites where the two chains are adjacent; the spin-uncoupled circuit has no opposite-spin terms, so its state is a product of an α\alpha and a β\beta part, and each part is prepared on its own register. The two outer rotations in Eq. (S1.6) act on a walker as a one-body rotation and keep it a Slater determinant. We therefore move them from the circuit to the walkers,

⟨ΨLUCJ|ϕ⟩=⟨Ψcirc|ϕ~⟩,|Ψcirc⟩=ei​J​e−K​|Φ0⟩,|ϕ~⟩=e−K​e−Kf​|ϕ⟩,\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{LUCJ}}|\phi\rangle=\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{circ}}|\tilde{\phi}\rangle,\qquad|\Psi_{\mathrm{circ}}\rangle=e^{iJ}e^{-K}|\Phi_{0}\rangle,\qquad|\tilde{\phi}\rangle=e^{-K}e^{-K_{\mathrm{f}}}|\phi\rangle, (S1.8)

and prepare only |Ψcirc⟩|\Psi_{\mathrm{circ}}\rangle on the processor: a determinant preparation by nearest-neighbor fermionic Givens rotations followed by the Jastrow layer, with no gates after it.

The rotated walkers ϕ~\tilde{\phi} are computed classically, and all overlaps reported in this work refer to the full state of Eq. (S1.6). In Figs. S1.5 and S1.6 we show the full ansatz, including the initial GHZ-type state preparation but excluding the random matchgates. Two-qubit gates are exclusively CZ\mathrm{CZ} gates, and arbitrary single-qubit rotations (represented as phased XZ gates in Willow’s native gate set) are denoted by empty squares. For the 14-orbital system, we prepared two circuits: a spin-coupled one (14o-C), in which both the GHZ preparation and the Jastrow CZ\mathrm{CZ} pairs couple the two spin registers, and a spin-uncoupled one (14o-U), with two independent spin registers. The 20-orbital system used the spin-uncoupled form.

Optimization of the circuit parameters.

We do not set the parameters following a coupled-cluster calculation, as originally proposed 48. Instead, we optimize them classically in two stages. First, we minimize the variational energy 4. Second, starting from the energy-optimized state, we teach the circuit a target wavefunction |Ψtgt⟩|\Psi_{\mathrm{tgt}}\rangle with FCI by minimizing the overlap loss function (Eq. (S2.33)) with walkers sampled by BS-UHF-guided phaseless AFQMC. The optimization uses Adam followed by geometric direct minimization with a line search 67. We keep the parameters with the lowest validation loss SS in a separate set of validation walkers; we never use reference energy, reference fidelity, or reference AFQMC results to choose them. Table S1.3 compares the two stages: teaching raises the variational energy by 14 and 26m​Eh~\textup{m}E_{\textup{h}}{} but brings the AFQMC error from about −11​m​Eh-11~\textup{m}E_{\textup{h}}{} to within 1​m​Eh1~\textup{m}E_{\textup{h}}{} for both active spaces.

S2 Quantum-classical hybrid QMC (QC-QMC) with machine-learned surrogate

S2.1 Overview of QC-QMC

We use phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) 77, 49, 30 to sample the imaginary-time projection

|Ψ0⟩∝limτ→∞e−τ​H​|Φ0⟩,|\Psi_{0}\rangle\propto\lim_{\tau\to\infty}e^{-\tau H}|\Phi_{0}\rangle, (S2.1)

where the initial state |Φ0⟩|\Phi_{0}\rangle has nonzero overlap with the ground state in the targeted symmetry sector. Introducing a trial wavefunction |ΨT⟩|\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}\rangle, the importance-sampled walker representation is

|Ψ⁡(τ)⟩≃∑i=1Nwwi​(τ)​|ϕi​(τ)⟩fT​(ϕi​(τ)),|\Psi(\tau)\rangle\simeq\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{w}}}w_{i}(\tau)\frac{|\phi_{i}(\tau)\rangle}{f_{\mathrm{T}}(\phi_{i}(\tau))}, (S2.2)
fT​(ϕ)=⟨ΨT|ϕ⟩f_{\mathrm{T}}(\phi)=\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}|\phi\rangle (S2.3)

where each walker |ϕi⟩|\phi_{i}\rangle is a Slater determinant and wiw_{i} is its importance-sampling weight. The hybrid quantum-classical quantum Monte Carlo (QC-QMC) uses a trial state |ΨT⟩|\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}\rangle that is prepared on a quantum processor to guide the QMC walk 30. A short-time factorization and Hubbard–Stratonovich transformation express the interacting propagator as an integral over one-body propagators. At each time step Δ​τ\Delta\tau, Gaussian auxiliary fields 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} are sampled and shifted by a trial-dependent force bias 𝐱¯i\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}, giving

|ϕi′⟩=BΔ​τ​(𝐱i−𝐱¯i)​|ϕi⟩.|\phi_{i}^{\prime}\rangle=B_{\Delta\tau}(\mathbf{x}_{i}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i})|\phi_{i}\rangle. (S2.4)

Because BΔ​τB_{\Delta\tau} is a one-body propagator, the updated walker remains a Slater determinant. The force bias reduces fluctuations in the importance weights. To control the fermionic phase problem, the phaseless approximation maintains nonnegative walker weights and applies the projection factor

max⁡{0,cos⁡Δ​θi},Δ​θi=arg⁡[fT​(ϕi′)fT​(ϕi)].\max\{0,\cos\Delta\theta_{i}\},\qquad\Delta\theta_{i}=\arg\!\left[\frac{f_{\mathrm{T}}(\phi_{i}^{\prime})}{f_{\mathrm{T}}(\phi_{i})}\right]. (S2.5)

This factor multiplies the nonnegative branching weight obtained from the importance-sampled propagation. The constraint introduces a systematic bias that depends on the trial wavefunction. The total energy is evaluated using the mixed estimator (local energy),

EL​(ϕ)\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{L}}(\phi) =⟨ΨT|H|ϕ⟩fT​(ϕ),\displaystyle=\frac{\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}|H|\phi\rangle}{f_{\mathrm{T}}(\phi)}, (S2.6)
E⁡(τ)\displaystyle E(\tau) =∑iwi​(τ)​Re⁡EL​(ϕi​(τ))∑iwi​(τ).\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i}w_{i}(\tau)\operatorname{Re}E_{\mathrm{L}}(\phi_{i}(\tau))}{\sum_{i}w_{i}(\tau)}.

The reported energy is estimated from the equilibrated imaginary-time sequence through reblocking analysis.

The trial-dependent quantities required by QC-QMC can be obtained from derivatives of the overlap with respect to the walker orbitals 34. This provides a common formulation for classical and quantum trials, and differentiable surrogate models. Let Φ\Phi denote the occupied-orbital matrix of the walker |ϕ⟩|\phi\rangle, and write fT​(Φ)=⟨ΨT|ϕ⟩f_{\mathrm{T}}(\Phi)=\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}|\phi\rangle. For a one-body operator A^=∑p​qAp​q​ap†​aq\hat{A}=\sum_{pq}A_{pq}a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}, define

FA​(t)=fT​(et​A​Φ).F_{A}(t)=f_{\mathrm{T}}(e^{tA}\Phi). (S2.7)

The action of et​A^e^{t\hat{A}} on a Slater determinant is equivalent to transforming its orbital matrix by et​Ae^{tA}. Consequently,

FA′​(0)\displaystyle F_{A}^{\prime}(0) =⟨ΨT|A^|ϕ⟩,\displaystyle=\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}|\hat{A}|\phi\rangle, (S2.8)
FA′′​(0)\displaystyle F_{A}^{\prime\prime}(0) =⟨ΨT|A^2|ϕ⟩.\displaystyle=\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}|\hat{A}^{2}|\phi\rangle.

The transformed determinant is generally unnormalized, so we must retain its normalization factors during differentiation. We write the factorized Hamiltonian as

H=Ecore+v^0−12​∑γv^γ2,v^γ=∑p​q(vγ)p​q​ap†​aq,H=E_{\mathrm{core}}+\hat{v}_{0}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\gamma}\hat{v}_{\gamma}^{2},\qquad\hat{v}_{\gamma}=\sum_{pq}(v_{\gamma})_{pq}a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}, (S2.9)

where v^0\hat{v}_{0} includes the one-body correction associated with the two-body factorization. For an auxiliary-field propagator containing Δ​τ​(xγ−x¯γ)​v^γ\sqrt{\Delta\tau}(x_{\gamma}-\bar{x}_{\gamma})\hat{v}_{\gamma}, the force bias and local energy are

x¯γ\displaystyle\bar{x}_{\gamma} =−Δ​τ​Fvγ′​(0)fT​(Φ),\displaystyle=-\sqrt{\Delta\tau}\,\frac{F_{v_{\gamma}}^{\prime}(0)}{f_{\mathrm{T}}(\Phi)}, (S2.10)
EL​(Φ)\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{L}}(\Phi) =Ecore+Fv0′​(0)fT​(Φ)−12​∑γFvγ′′​(0)fT​(Φ).\displaystyle=E_{\mathrm{core}}+\frac{F_{v_{0}}^{\prime}(0)}{f_{\mathrm{T}}(\Phi)}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\gamma}\frac{F_{v_{\gamma}}^{\prime\prime}(0)}{f_{\mathrm{T}}(\Phi)}. (S2.11)

Thus, first derivatives determine the force bias and one-body energy, while second derivatives determine the remaining contribution to the local energy. In QC-QMC, these derivatives can be evaluated by classically computing the shadow-overlap estimator while holding the measurement record fixed. The same construction applies when the overlap estimator is replaced by a trained surrogate fθf_{\theta}, yielding approximate force biases and local energies from its derivatives. Here the model parameters θ\theta remain fixed, and differentiation includes the full dependence of the model on the walker orbitals.

S2.2 Matchgate shadow estimates and noise floor

Overlap estimation from shadows.

Let |χ⟩=(|𝟎⟩+|ΨT⟩)/2|\chi\rangle=(|\mathbf{0}\rangle+|\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}\rangle)/\sqrt{2} and write ρ=|χ⟩​⟨χ|\rho=|\chi\rangle\!\langle\chi|. For any η\eta-electron determinant |ϕ⟩|\phi\rangle, its overlap with |ΨT⟩|\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}\rangle is determined via 30

⟨ΨT|ϕ⟩=2​tr⁡(ρ⁡|ϕ⟩​⟨𝟎|).\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}|\phi\rangle=2\tr(\rho|\phi\rangle\!\langle\mathbf{0}|). (S2.12)

It was shown that MM such overlaps can be estimated to additive ϵ\epsilon precision from 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡(N)​log⁡(M)/ϵ2)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N}\log(N)\log(M)/\epsilon^{2}) matchgate shadow samples 71. That work also gave an algorithm with runtime 𝒪⁡(N4)\mathcal{O}(N^{4}) per sample per determinant to evaluate the overlap estimator. This is based on polynomial interpolation, which exhibits numerical instability 38. We introduce two new algorithms with improved 𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}) runtime, based on a Paige–Van Loan reduction 55 and a generalized eigenvalue solver 45, respectively. Note that independent and concurrent work also derived a cubic-scaling algorithm that, similar to our first contribution (Sec. S4), applies to almost all overlap instances 51. Our second contribution, however, applies to all instances, albeit with a slightly larger runtime prefactor. We describe all algorithms and prove their properties in Supplementary Sec. S4. For the numerical implementation of these routines, we make bespoke refinements based on system size and GPU architecture to maximize performance in practice; the details are recorded in Supplementary Sec. S4.4.

Fig. S2.1 compares our implementation with the previous interpolation scheme 71. For benchmarking purposes, we re-implemented the interpolation scheme with Chebyshev polynomials 80 and compared it against our kernels. We compared the overlap and force bias time cost (Fig. S2.1a) and the end-to-end time cost for a 16-qubit Ni complex in a full orbital space by making use of the virtual correlation energy (VCE) algorithm 34 (Fig. S2.1b). Apart from the acceleration, we also note that the traditional interpolation scheme loses accuracy as the system grows: its median per-pair relative error rises from 1×10−131\times 10^{-13} at 16 qubits to 5×10−95\times 10^{-9} at 40 qubits, and its maximum from 6×10−126\times 10^{-12} to 1.5×10−61.5\times 10^{-6}, while ours stays below 10−1210^{-12} (Fig. S2.1c). This reflects the poor conditioning of interpolation at real nodes followed by conversion to the monomial basis 38; interpolation in the Fourier basis, which we use, does not suffer from it (Supplementary Sec. S4.4). Within our own algorithm, we also compared the derivative calculation time cost between automatic differentiation and closed-form derivatives for the force bias and the local energy. We also note that for the single-walker benchmark of ref. 51 (40 qubits, 10510^{5} snapshots, one propagation step), with a reported 737 s on ten AMD EPYC 7763 cores, our implementation takes 37 s on one MI250X GCD, reflecting the benefit of implementing fast matchgate shadow algorithms on GPUs. Beyond cost, our overlap algorithm applies to all instances, so no near-singular snapshots need to be discarded (Supplementary Sec. S4). The algorithmic choices behind these gains are described in Supplementary Secs. S4.4 and S4.5.

Noisy classical-shadow estimates.

The classical-shadow estimates of the overlaps between the prepared state |ΨT⟩|\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}\rangle and a set of walker single determinants {|ϕw⟩}\{|\phi_{w}\rangle\} are noisy data,

yw=1Nc​∑c=1Ncy^w,c,𝔼⁡[y^w,c]=λ0​⟨ΨT|ϕw⟩,y_{w}=\frac{1}{N_{c}}\sum_{c=1}^{N_{c}}\hat{y}_{w,c},\qquad\mathbb{E}\bigl[\hat{y}_{w,c}\bigr]=\lambda_{0}\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}|\phi_{w}\rangle, (S2.13)

where y^w,c\hat{y}_{w,c} is the estimate from circuit cc, with its shots averaged. The common scalar λ0\lambda_{0} is the effect of the hardware noise after twirling by matchgate shadows, assuming Markovian, gate-independent errors 27. In practice, the device noise does not obey those assumptions exactly, but we can nonetheless implicitly fit for it. We absorb it into our fitting parameters below. Each label ywy_{w} in Eq. (S2.13) is an unbiased estimate, with a statistical error that decreases as circuits are added. Measurement noise therefore comes from two sources: a finite number of shots for a given circuit and hardware noise. This is in addition to the intrinsic shadow error due to a finite number of circuits. We split the walkers into training and validation sets and compute every label (overlap) from the same circuits, so both sets share the same realization of measurement noise. To quantify these sources of error, we divide the NcN_{c} circuits into nn groups (the result is insensitive to the group size once each group contains at least 100 circuits and beyond 500 shots per circuit in our practice), and denote the label obtained from group gg by yw(g)y_{w}^{(g)}. The standard error of ywy_{w} is

σw2=1n⁡(n−1)​∑g=1n|yw(g)−yw|2\sigma_{w}^{2}=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{g=1}^{n}\bigl|y_{w}^{(g)}-y_{w}\bigr|^{2} (S2.14)

which measures the statistical uncertainty of the labels, from both the random measurement circuits and the finite number of shots; as such, it does not exhibit systematic errors common to all groups. For spin-uncoupled circuits, yw=ywα​ywβy_{w}=y_{w}^{\alpha}y_{w}^{\beta}, so we apply Eq. (S2.14) to each spin-sector and combine the two to first order,

σw2=|ywβ|2​σw,α2+|ywα|2​σw,β2+2​Re​[(ywα)∗​ywβ​cw],\sigma_{w}^{2}=|y_{w}^{\beta}|^{2}\sigma_{w,\alpha}^{2}+|y_{w}^{\alpha}|^{2}\sigma_{w,\beta}^{2}+2\,\mathrm{Re}\bigl[(y_{w}^{\alpha})^{*}y_{w}^{\beta}\,c_{w}\bigr], (S2.15)

where cw=1n⁡(n−1)​∑g(ywα,(g)−ywα)​(ywβ,(g)−ywβ)∗c_{w}=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{g}(y_{w}^{\alpha,(g)}-y_{w}^{\alpha})(y_{w}^{\beta,(g)}-y_{w}^{\beta})^{*} is the covariance of the two half labels, kept because both halves are measured in the same circuits. In practice, we evaluate σw\sigma_{w} by a jackknife over the same groups, which agrees with Eq. (S2.15) to leading order in 1/n1/n. We define the noise floor on the validation walkers,

F=∥σ∥val∥y∥val=(∑w∈valσw2∑w∈val|yw|2)1/2.F=\frac{\lVert\sigma\rVert_{\mathrm{val}}}{\lVert y\rVert_{\mathrm{val}}}=\left(\frac{\sum_{w\in\mathrm{val}}\sigma_{w}^{2}}{\sum_{w\in\mathrm{val}}|y_{w}|^{2}}\right)^{1/2}. (S2.16)

Fig. S2.2 shows the convergence of the noise floor of hydrogen chains and different LUCJ circuits for [Fe2S2(SCH3)4]2- (including state preparation and the matchgate shadow measurements).

For a given surrogate Ψθ\Psi_{\theta} with parameters θ\theta, we measure its fit by

v=(∑w∈val|λ⁡⟨Ψθ|ϕw⟩−yw|2∑w∈val|yw|2)1/2,λ=∑w∈train⟨Ψθ|ϕw⟩∗​yw∑w∈train|⟨Ψθ|ϕw⟩|2,v=\left(\frac{\sum_{w\in\mathrm{val}}\bigl|\lambda\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\phi_{w}\rangle-y_{w}\bigr|^{2}}{\sum_{w\in\mathrm{val}}|y_{w}|^{2}}\right)^{1/2},\qquad\lambda=\frac{\sum_{w\in\mathrm{train}}\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\phi_{w}\rangle^{*}y_{w}}{\sum_{w\in\mathrm{train}}|\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\phi_{w}\rangle|^{2}}, (S2.17)

where λ\lambda is the least-squares estimate of λ0\lambda_{0} on the training walkers, so that no parameter is adjusted to the validation labels. Writing yw=λ0​⟨ΨT|ϕw⟩+ϵwy_{w}=\lambda_{0}\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}|\phi_{w}\rangle+\epsilon_{w} with 𝔼⁡[|ϵw|2]=σw2\mathbb{E}\bigl[|\epsilon_{w}|^{2}\bigr]=\sigma_{w}^{2}, the circuit state itself gives 𝔼⁡[v2]≃F2\mathbb{E}[v^{2}]\simeq F^{2}: from the labels alone, no surrogate can be shown to agree with the circuit state more closely than FF. A surrogate at relative distance dd from the noise-free labels gives 𝔼⁡[v2]≃d2+F2\mathbb{E}[v^{2}]\simeq d^{2}+F^{2} when the noise is independent of the surrogate. Therefore, we define the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of a starting state with validation error v0v_{0} as

SNR=v02−F2F≃dF,\mathrm{SNR}=\frac{\sqrt{v_{0}^{2}-F^{2}}}{F}\simeq\frac{d}{F}, (S2.18)

which measures how much of its error the labels can resolve. Because the training and validation walkers share the same hardware noise source, training can lower vv below FF by fitting to the noise; we therefore use v≤Fv\leq F as a stopping criterion.

S2.3 Surrogate models and training strategy

During QC-QMC, we replace the shadow estimator with a differentiable model trained on the shadow estimates (Fig. S2.3), which returns the overlap and its first and second derivatives for any walker at a cost independent of the number of snapshots. In this work we used two such models separately: a backflow neural quantum surrogate for the hydrogen chains and a nonorthogonal configuration interaction (NOCI) surrogate for [Fe2S2(SCH3)4]2-. We deliberately start the NQS from a random initialization, with no classical initial guess, so that the hydrogen-chain trial is learned from the noisy measurements alone. The NOCI surrogate instead starts from a cheap classical NOCI calculation. For harder problems, they can be combined, for example by starting from a NOCI expansion and letting a backflow network learn walker-dependent corrections to its orbitals, so that the chemical prior sets the starting point and the network adds flexibility and expressivity where the data can resolve it.

Backflow neural quantum surrogate.

We propose a neural quantum surrogate, which returns a single determinant whose orbitals depend on the input walker ϕ=(ϕα,ϕβ)\phi=(\phi_{\alpha},\phi_{\beta}) through its spin projectors,

fθ​(ϕ)=∏σ∈{α,β}det[Gθσ​(Pϕα,Pϕβ)†​ϕσ],Pϕσ=ϕσ​(ϕσ†​ϕσ)−1​ϕσ†,\begin{split}f_{\theta}(\phi)&=\prod_{\sigma\in\{\alpha,\beta\}}\det\!\left[G^{\sigma}_{\theta}(P^{\alpha}_{\phi},P^{\beta}_{\phi})^{\dagger}\phi_{\sigma}\right],\\ P^{\sigma}_{\phi}&=\phi_{\sigma}\left(\phi_{\sigma}^{\dagger}\phi_{\sigma}\right)^{-1}\phi_{\sigma}^{\dagger},\end{split} (S2.19)

where the function

Gθσ\displaystyle G^{\sigma}_{\theta} :Gr⁡(ηα,N)×Gr⁡(ηβ,N)→ℂN×ησ,\displaystyle:\mathrm{Gr}(\eta_{\alpha},N)\times\mathrm{Gr}(\eta_{\beta},N)\to\mathbb{C}^{N\times\eta_{\sigma}}, (S2.20)
Gr⁡(η,N)\displaystyle\mathrm{Gr}(\eta,N) ={P∈ℂN×N:P2=P=P†,tr(P)=η},\displaystyle=\{P\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}:P^{2}=P=P^{\dagger},\tr(P)=\eta\},

outputs a set of ϕ\phi-dependent orbitals. The network sees the walker only through its projector Pϕα⊕PϕβP^{\alpha}_{\phi}\oplus P^{\beta}_{\phi}, a point on the complex Grassmann manifold Gr⁡(ηα,N)×Gr⁡(ηβ,N)\mathrm{Gr}(\eta_{\alpha},N)\times\mathrm{Gr}(\eta_{\beta},N). PϕσP^{\sigma}_{\phi} is invariant under ϕσ→ϕσ​Uσ\phi_{\sigma}\to\phi_{\sigma}U_{\sigma}, so the surrogate transforms as an overlap with a fixed state, fθ​(ϕ​U)=det(Uα)​det(Uβ)​fθ​(ϕ)f_{\theta}(\phi U)=\det(U_{\alpha})\det(U_{\beta})\,f_{\theta}(\phi). For singlet calculation, we use spin projection where the walkers are spin-restricted (ϕα=ϕβ\phi_{\alpha}=\phi_{\beta}, hence Pϕα=PϕβP^{\alpha}_{\phi}=P^{\beta}_{\phi}), the network can just take a single projector as input while still outputting separate α\alpha and β\beta orbitals, which allows for spin-broken determinants.

Derivatives of the neural surrogate.

We take every derivative along a unitary orbital rotation, ΦB​(s)=ei​s​B​Φ\Phi_{B}(s)=e^{isB}\Phi with BB Hermitian and ss real, and define

⟨B^⟩θ=−i∂sfθ(ΦB(s))|s=0fθ​(Φ),⟨B^2⟩θ=−∂s2fθ(ΦB(s))|s=0fθ​(Φ),\langle\hat{B}\rangle_{\theta}=\frac{-i\,\partial_{s}f_{\theta}(\Phi_{B}(s))|_{s=0}}{f_{\theta}(\Phi)},\qquad\langle\hat{B}^{2}\rangle_{\theta}=\frac{-\partial_{s}^{2}f_{\theta}(\Phi_{B}(s))|_{s=0}}{f_{\theta}(\Phi)}, (S2.21)

for the one-body operator v0v_{0} and the Cholesky vectors LγL_{\gamma} (in Eq. (S2.11), vγ=i​Lγv_{\gamma}=iL_{\gamma}). Only derivatives up to second order are needed, so we use ΦB​(s)=(I+i​s​B−12​s2​B2)​Φ\Phi_{B}(s)=(I+isB-\tfrac{1}{2}s^{2}B^{2})\Phi. All derivatives are obtained by automatic differentiation of the scalar overlap. One reverse-mode pass gives

Gp​q=1fθ​(Φ)​∑k(∂fθ∂Φp​k​Φq​k−∂fθ∂Φp​k∗​Φq​k∗),G_{pq}=\frac{1}{f_{\theta}(\Phi)}\sum_{k}\left(\frac{\partial f_{\theta}}{\partial\Phi_{pk}}\Phi_{qk}-\frac{\partial f_{\theta}}{\partial\Phi^{*}_{pk}}\Phi^{*}_{qk}\right), (S2.22)

with ⟨B^⟩θ=∑p​qBp​q​Gp​q\langle\hat{B}\rangle_{\theta}=\sum_{pq}B_{pq}G_{pq} for real symmetric BB, so the force bias along every Cholesky vector follows from a single pass. For a fixed state, the second term vanishes, and GG is the mixed one-body Green’s function. The one-body energy uses one forward-mode derivative along hh. We evaluate ⟨L^γ2⟩θ\langle\hat{L}_{\gamma}^{2}\rangle_{\theta} for each Cholesky vector by nested forward-mode derivatives along ΦLγ​(s)\Phi_{L_{\gamma}}(s).

Nonorthogonal configuration interaction surrogate.

The surrogate can also be built from a quantum-chemistry wavefunction ansatz, which brings chemical prior knowledge into the model and serves as a good initial guess for training. Here we use NOCI 36, 18, a linear combination of KK Slater determinants whose orbitals are optimized independently and need not be orthogonal between determinants,

|Ψθ⟩=∑k=1Kck​|Dk⟩,fθ​(ϕ)=⟨Ψθ|ϕ⟩=∑k=1Kck∗​∏σ∈{α,β}det(Wk​σ†​ϕσ),|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle=\sum_{k=1}^{K}c_{k}|D_{k}\rangle,\qquad f_{\theta}(\phi)=\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\phi\rangle=\sum_{k=1}^{K}c_{k}^{*}\prod_{\sigma\in\{\alpha,\beta\}}\det\!\left(W_{k\sigma}^{\dagger}\phi_{\sigma}\right), (S2.23)

where Wk​σ∈ℂN×ησW_{k\sigma}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times\eta_{\sigma}} holds the occupied orbitals of spin σ\sigma in |Dk⟩|D_{k}\rangle and θ={ck,Wk​σ}\theta=\{c_{k},W_{k\sigma}\}. Unlike the backflow surrogate, |Ψθ⟩|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle is a fixed state that does not depend on the walker. The α\alpha and β\beta orbitals of each determinant are independent, so every |Dk⟩|D_{k}\rangle may break spin symmetry, as a broken-symmetry unrestricted Hartree–Fock (BS-UHF) determinant does. Each determinant is parameterized by a Thouless chart 63 around a fixed origin Ok​σ∈ℂN×ησO_{k\sigma}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times\eta_{\sigma}},

Wk​σ=Ok​σ+Vk​σ​Zk​σ,Zk​σ∈ℂ(N−ησ)×ησ,W_{k\sigma}=O_{k\sigma}+V_{k\sigma}Z_{k\sigma},\qquad Z_{k\sigma}\in\mathbb{C}^{(N-\eta_{\sigma})\times\eta_{\sigma}}, (S2.24)

where the columns of Vk​σV_{k\sigma} form an orthonormal basis of the orthogonal complement of the columns of Ok​σO_{k\sigma} (Vk​σ†​Ok​σ=0V_{k\sigma}^{\dagger}O_{k\sigma}=0). Every determinant with nonzero overlap with the origin is reached by some Zk​σZ_{k\sigma}, up to a norm and phase that ckc_{k} absorbs. Occupied–occupied rotations, which change only the norm and phase of |Dk⟩|D_{k}\rangle, are excluded, and no orthonormality constraint is imposed. For a walker with orbital matrices Φσ\Phi_{\sigma} define, for each determinant,

Sk​σ=Wk​σ†​Φσ,Θk​σ=Φσ​Sk​σ−1​Wk​σ†,ok=ck∗​∏σdetSk​σ,S_{k\sigma}=W_{k\sigma}^{\dagger}\Phi_{\sigma},\qquad\Theta_{k\sigma}=\Phi_{\sigma}S_{k\sigma}^{-1}W_{k\sigma}^{\dagger},\qquad o_{k}=c_{k}^{*}\prod_{\sigma}\det S_{k\sigma}, (S2.25)

so that fθ​(Φ)=∑kokf_{\theta}(\Phi)=\sum_{k}o_{k}. Here (Θk​σ)q​p=⟨Dk|ap​σ†​aq​σ|ϕ⟩/⟨Dk|ϕ⟩(\Theta_{k\sigma})_{qp}=\langle D_{k}|a_{p\sigma}^{\dagger}a_{q\sigma}|\phi\rangle/\langle D_{k}|\phi\rangle is the mixed one-body Green’s function of determinant kk (in transposed form), and Θk​σ2=Θk​σ\Theta_{k\sigma}^{2}=\Theta_{k\sigma}. Applying Jacobi’s formula ∂tdetM=detM​tr⁡(M−1​∂tM)\partial_{t}\det M=\det M\,\tr(M^{-1}\partial_{t}M) to the directional derivatives of Eq. (S2.8) for a spin-free one-body operator A^\hat{A} gives

FA′​(0)\displaystyle F_{A}^{\prime}(0) =∑kok​∑σtr⁡(A​Θk​σ),\displaystyle=\sum_{k}o_{k}\sum_{\sigma}\tr\!\left(A\Theta_{k\sigma}\right), (S2.26)
FA′′​(0)\displaystyle F_{A}^{\prime\prime}(0) =∑kok​{[∑σtr⁡(A​Θk​σ)]2+∑σtr⁡[A​Θk​σ​A​(1−Θk​σ)]},\displaystyle=\sum_{k}o_{k}\Bigl\{\Bigl[\sum_{\sigma}\tr\!\left(A\Theta_{k\sigma}\right)\Bigr]^{2}+\sum_{\sigma}\tr\!\left[A\Theta_{k\sigma}A\left(1-\Theta_{k\sigma}\right)\right]\Bigr\},

which is the generalized Wick theorem applied to each determinant. Inserted into Eq. (S2.11), Eq. (S2.26) makes the force bias and local energy overlap-weighted averages over determinants, with weights ok/fθ​(Φ)o_{k}/f_{\theta}(\Phi). All quantities are closed-form, and no automatic differentiation is needed during propagation. The half-rotated operators Wk​σ†​vγW_{k\sigma}^{\dagger}v_{\gamma} are computed once per trial, so the cost per walker is O⁡(K​Nγ​N​η2)O(KN_{\gamma}N\eta^{2}), set by the exchange term, where NγN_{\gamma} is the number of auxiliary fields.

For K=1K=1 the origin is the BS-UHF determinant. For K≥2K\geq 2 the origins and coefficients come from a variation-after-projection (VAP) calculation 36, which uses the Hamiltonian only and no shadow data. The orbitals minimize the singlet-projected energy

E0​[Ψ]=⟨Ψ|H^​P^0|Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|P^0|Ψ⟩,P^0=12​∫0πd​β​sin⁡β​e−i​β​S^y,E_{0}[\Psi]=\frac{\langle\Psi|\hat{H}\hat{P}_{0}|\Psi\rangle}{\langle\Psi|\hat{P}_{0}|\Psi\rangle},\qquad\hat{P}_{0}=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi}\!d\beta\,\sin\beta\,e^{-i\beta\hat{S}_{y}}, (S2.27)

where P^0\hat{P}_{0} projects Sz=0S_{z}=0 states onto total spin S=0S=0, and the integral is evaluated by quadrature in β\beta. For fixed orbitals, the coefficients are the lowest solution of the projected generalized eigenproblem ∑l⟨Dk|H^​P^0|Dl⟩​cl=E​∑l⟨Dk|P^0|Dl⟩​cl\sum_{l}\langle D_{k}|\hat{H}\hat{P}_{0}|D_{l}\rangle c_{l}=E\sum_{l}\langle D_{k}|\hat{P}_{0}|D_{l}\rangle c_{l}. We add new determinants by starting from a perturbed copy of existing ones, and we reoptimize the whole expansion at every stage. The QMC trial and the starting point of the learning procedure are the unprojected state (Eq. (S2.23)) with the VAP orbitals and coefficients.

Machine learning quantum measurements from a NOCI prior.

The labels ywy_{w}, their standard errors σw\sigma_{w}, the validation error vv, the noise floor FF and the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) are defined in Sec. S2.2. The SNR of the starting state, Eq. (S2.18), compares the part of its error that the labels can resolve with the label noise, and we use it to decide how many parameters to fit. If SNR>1\mathrm{SNR}>1, the labels resolve the error of the starting state and we teach all parameters (i). If SNR≤1\mathrm{SNR}\leq 1, the starting state already agrees with the labels to within their noise; fitting all orbital parameters would mostly fit the noise, so we keep the VAP orbitals and refit only the KK coefficients (ii). The walkers come in pairs p=(ϕp​0,ϕp​1)p=(\phi_{p0},\phi_{p1}) taken from the same random walk at two imaginary times, and both walkers of every pair are labeled.

(i) Teaching. Starting from the VAP state (Zk​σ=0Z_{k\sigma}=0), all orbital parameters Zk​σZ_{k\sigma} and coefficients ckc_{k} are trained by minimizing the overlap error and overlap ratios. We optimize with Adam and keep the first checkpoint with v≤Fv\leq F, or the one with the lowest vv if FF is never reached.

(ii) Coefficient refit. With the orbitals frozen at the VAP origins, Eq. (S2.23) is linear in ck∗c_{k}^{*}, fθ​(ϕw)=∑k𝒪w​k​ck∗f_{\theta}(\phi_{w})=\sum_{k}\mathcal{O}_{wk}c_{k}^{*} with 𝒪w​k=∏σdet(Ok​σ†​ϕw​σ)\mathcal{O}_{wk}=\prod_{\sigma}\det(O_{k\sigma}^{\dagger}\phi_{w\sigma}). Absorbing the global label factor into the coefficients turns the fit into a linear least-squares problem over both walkers of every training pair,

c∗=arg​minx∈ℂK∑w∈train|∑k𝒪w​kxk−yw|2,c^{*}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in\mathbb{C}^{K}}\sum_{w\in\mathrm{train}}\Bigl|\sum_{k}\mathcal{O}_{wk}x_{k}-y_{w}\Bigr|^{2}, (S2.28)

whose solution is unique when 𝒪\mathcal{O} has full column rank and needs no optimizer or checkpoint selection.

The training set consists of NtrainN_{\mathrm{train}} walker pairs drawn from UHF-guided phaseless AFQMC, one time step apart,

𝒟={(ϕi,ϕi′)}i=1Ntrain,ϕi=ϕ⁡(τi),ϕi′=ϕ⁡(τi+Δ​τ).\mathcal{D}=\{(\phi_{i},\phi_{i}^{\prime})\}_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{train}}},\qquad\phi_{i}=\phi(\tau_{i}),\quad\phi_{i}^{\prime}=\phi(\tau_{i}+\Delta\tau). (S2.29)

We find no significant difference between training on walkers sampled under UHF guidance and on walkers sampled under correlated-trial guidance, so the training set can be generated with an inexpensive classical trial before the correlated trial is available. Each label is the averaged shadow overlap of the trial state with the walker,

y⁡(ϕ)=1S​∑s=1So^s​(ϕ),𝔼⁡[o^s​(ϕ)]=⟨ΨT|ϕ⟩,y(\phi)=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\hat{o}_{s}(\phi),\qquad\mathbb{E}\big[\hat{o}_{s}(\phi)\big]=\langle\Psi_{T}|\phi\rangle, (S2.30)

where o^s​(ϕ)\hat{o}_{s}(\phi) is the overlap estimator from the ss-th of SS shadow snapshots. Labels are divided by the modulus of the largest training label, and the model output is divided by its modulus on the same walker,

y~​(ϕ)=y⁡(ϕ)|y⁡(ϕref)|,f~θ​(ϕ)=Ψθ​(ϕ)|Ψθ​(ϕref)|,ϕref=arg​maxϕ∈𝒯⁡|y⁡(ϕ)|,\tilde{y}(\phi)=\frac{y(\phi)}{|y(\phi_{\mathrm{ref}})|},\qquad\tilde{f}_{\theta}(\phi)=\frac{\Psi_{\theta}(\phi)}{|\Psi_{\theta}(\phi_{\mathrm{ref}})|},\qquad\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\phi\in\mathcal{T}}|y(\phi)|, (S2.31)

where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the set of 2​Ntrain2N_{\mathrm{train}} training walkers (both members of every pair). The loss is a log-cosh penalty on the real and imaginary parts of the complex residual rθ​(ϕ)=f~θ​(ϕ)−y~​(ϕ)r_{\theta}(\phi)=\tilde{f}_{\theta}(\phi)-\tilde{y}(\phi), each scaled by its spread over the training set,

ℒov​(θ)=12​Ntrain​∑ϕ∈𝒯[ln⁡cosh⁡Re⁡rθ​(ϕ)sR+ln⁡cosh⁡Im⁡rθ​(ϕ)sI],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ov}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{2N_{\mathrm{train}}}\sum_{\phi\in\mathcal{T}}\left[\ln\cosh\frac{\operatorname{Re}r_{\theta}(\phi)}{s_{\mathrm{R}}}+\ln\cosh\frac{\operatorname{Im}r_{\theta}(\phi)}{s_{\mathrm{I}}}\right], (S2.32)

with sRs_{\mathrm{R}} and sIs_{\mathrm{I}} the standard deviations of Re⁡y~\operatorname{Re}\tilde{y} and Im⁡y~\operatorname{Im}\tilde{y} over 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Each surrogate is trained by minimizing an overlap term and, optionally, a pair-ratio term,

ℒ⁡(θ)=ℒov​(θ)+β​ℒR​(θ).\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ov}}(\theta)+\beta\,\mathcal{L}_{R}(\theta). (S2.33)

The overlap term penalizes the residual between the surrogate and the labels over the training walkers, after the unknown global factor of the labels is removed, either by normalizing labels and surrogate at a reference walker or by a least-squares complex scale. The ratio term exploits the fact that the two walkers of a pair are one time step apart and share the same shadow snapshots, so most of the noise cancels in their ratio Ri=y⁡(ϕi′)/y⁡(ϕi)R_{i}=y(\phi_{i}^{\prime})/y(\phi_{i}). With Rθ,i=fθ​(ϕi′)/fθ​(ϕi)R_{\theta,i}=f_{\theta}(\phi_{i}^{\prime})/f_{\theta}(\phi_{i}),

ℒR​(θ)=∑iωi​[(ln⁡|Rθ,i|−ln⁡|Ri|sln)2+(wrap⁡(arg⁡Rθ,i−arg⁡Ri)sarg)2]∑iωi,\mathcal{L}_{R}(\theta)=\frac{\sum_{i}\omega_{i}\Bigl[\Bigl(\frac{\ln|R_{\theta,i}|-\ln|R_{i}|}{s_{\ln}}\Bigr)^{2}+\Bigl(\frac{\operatorname{wrap}(\arg R_{\theta,i}-\arg R_{i})}{s_{\arg}}\Bigr)^{2}\Bigr]}{\sum_{i}\omega_{i}}, (S2.34)

where the weights ωi\omega_{i} suppress pairs whose label ratio is dominated by noise. These ratios set the importance weights and the phaseless angle of the walker. One can also employ derivative information including force bias and local energies to perform Sobolev training. We choose the checkpoint on walkers not used for training, with the noise floor FF as the reference.

S3 Benchmarks and error analysis

S3.1 Noiseless simulations

We examine how shadow-reconstructed trial states and AFQMC energies depend on measurement budget and simulated readout noise for hydrogen chains with 8, 12, and 16 qubits. Simulated results and walker-overlap distributions are shown at interatomic spacings of r=1.6r=1.6, 2.42.4, and 3.03.0 Bohr. Figure S3.1 shows the AFQMC energy deviation against the number of circuits for noiseless simulated shadows, and the walker-overlap magnitudes at each bond length.

S3.2 Simulated readout errors

Figure S3.2 illustrates this in simulation for UHF trials on 8, 12 and 16 qubits, where the full coefficient vector can be compared with shadow estimates under symmetric readout flips with probability pp up to 10%, a range that includes the readout errors of the device (Fig. S1.1). Without noise, the coefficient error falls as N−1/2N^{-1/2} with the number of shadows NN. Readout noise leaves a floor in the absolute coefficient error that rises with pp, but the normalized infidelity, which is insensitive to a global factor, keeps decreasing with NN, more slowly only at the largest pp. Readout noise therefore acts mainly as a global attenuation, which Eq. (S2.13) absorbs into λ0\lambda_{0}. Figure S3.3 carries the same simulation through to the energy, using the shadow-estimated state as the AFQMC trial for 8 and 12 qubits. Because AFQMC uses the trial only through overlap ratios, a global factor cancels (Section S1.2), and the energy error is set mainly by the number of shadows rather than by the readout noise. With 9×1059\times 10^{5} or more shadows, the error is below 1 m​Eh\textup{m}E_{\textup{h}} at every flip probability shown, up to p=10%p=10\%, for both sizes; at 8 qubits, 1.6×1051.6\times 10^{5} shadows already suffice at every pp, and 3×1043\times 10^{4} for p≤5%p\leq 5\%.

S3.3 Experimental convergence of matchgate-shadow overlaps

Figure S3.4 shows how hardware estimates of the walker overlaps for the hydrogen chains converge with the number of circuits and with the shots per circuit, and how two choices in the experiment affect this convergence. Parity postselection (Section S1.2) lowers the relative overlap error at 24 qubits by a factor of about 1.7 at every budget shown. Spin-blocked shadows (Section S5.2) lower it at 32 qubits by a factor of about 1.6 relative to full-spin shadows, consistent with their shallower circuits (Fig. S1.2). At a fixed number of circuits, all curves fall as S−1/2S^{-1/2} with the number of shots SS, so both choices reduce the prefactor rather than changing the rate. A factor of 1.6–1.7 in error corresponds to roughly 2.5–3 times fewer shots for the same accuracy. Figure S3.5 compares the overlaps estimated from the hardware shadows with their ideal value. The experiment reproduces both the distribution of walker-overlap magnitudes and the overlap ratios of individual walker pairs.

S3.4 NQS training, error, and cost analysis

For each chain length (8, 16, 24, 32 and 40 qubits, i.e. H4–H20) we train ten neural-network trial wavefunctions on classical-shadow overlap data. The network maps a walker ϕ=(ϕα,ϕβ)\phi=(\phi_{\alpha},\phi_{\beta}) to walker-dependent orbitals ψσ​(ϕ,θ)∈ℂn×nσ\psi_{\sigma}(\phi;\theta)\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n_{\sigma}} and returns the single-determinant overlap

Ψθ​(ϕ)=det[ψα​(ϕ,θ)†​ϕα]​det[ψβ​(ϕ,θ)†​ϕβ].\Psi_{\theta}(\phi)=\det\!\big[\psi_{\alpha}(\phi;\theta)^{\dagger}\phi_{\alpha}\big]\,\det\!\big[\psi_{\beta}(\phi;\theta)^{\dagger}\phi_{\beta}\big]. (S3.1)

One QMC run propagates 640 walkers for 5,000 blocks of 25 steps. Each step requires the trial overlap and force bias of every walker, and each block requires one local-energy evaluation. In conventional QC-QMC, every overlap, force bias, and local energy is averaged over all NsN_{\mathrm{s}} snapshots with GPU matchgate-shadow kernels. Its cost is the measured cost of one block on the full shadow data, multiplied by 5000. At 8 and 16 qubits, the circuit counts are those at which brute-force shadow AFQMC reproduces the noiseless reference within chemical accuracy: 100 and 2,500 circuits at 500 shots, Ns=5×104N_{\mathrm{s}}=5\times 10^{4} and 1.25×1061.25\times 10^{6}. For the surrogate, we count three parts: the shadow labels, network training, and the AFQMC run with the trained network. The labels are the overlaps of 2​N+51202N+5120 walkers: both walkers of the NN training pairs and of 2,560 stopping-set pairs, each averaged over all NsN_{\mathrm{s}} snapshots with the same kernels. For the surrogate training, each orbital pp is a token whose features are the real and imaginary parts of the ppth row of PP (Eq. (S2.19)). The tokens are linearly embedded to width dd with a learned orbital embedding, processed by a transformer encoder (SiLU activations) and a full linear output head, with Xavier-normal initialization scaled by 0.01. We perform 10 independent trainings, and each trained network must pass a health check before its AFQMC run. The check uses no benchmark energy and is evaluated on an external panel of validation walkers not used in training or early stopping. A network fails if its validation error exceeds the label noise floor, v/F>1v/F>1. Among the networks in a run that pass, we also remove a network if its mean local energy from the trained model exceeds the median over those networks by more than 1.6 mHa (chemical accuracy); only differences between networks enter, so we use no reference energy.

In the AFQMC run, the trained network returns the overlap, and automatic differentiation computes its force bias and local energy. Costs are given in GPU hours on OLCF Frontier, where one GPU is one graphics compute die (GCD) of an AMD Instinct MI250X accelerator (four accelerators and eight GCDs per node). We count only these trial-wavefunction evaluations, since walker propagation costs the same in both methods. The shadow data comprise NsN_{\mathrm{s}} snapshots, the number of circuits times the shots per circuit (Supplementary Table S3.1).

S3.5 Low-spin state of [Fe2S2(SCH3)4]2-

For [Fe2S2(SCH3)4]2- we use the geometry reported previously 61. This 40-qubit Hamiltonian is reconstructed following the previously reported active-space procedure 41, available at https://github.com/jiangtong1000/fe2s2-hamiltonian-reconstruction-. The 28-qubit Hamiltonian is the previously reported (18e, 14o) model 39. We optimized compact NOCI expansions by variation after spin projection (VAP), in which the orbitals and coefficients of KK determinants minimize the energy of the spin-projected state. For each K∈{2,4,8}K\in\{2,4,8\} we ran five optimizations from different random seeds, grouped those that converged to the same state, and used each distinct state as the trial in phaseless AFQMC (Fig. S3.7, left and middle). Expansions are grown by doubling: each added determinant starts as a copy of an existing one rotated by small random angles (principal angles of 4–12∘) with zero coefficient, after which all orbitals and coefficients are re-optimized. For 20o, each seed is an independent lineage: starting from the spin-projected broken-symmetry UHF determinant (K=1K=1), it is doubled to K=2K=2, 4, and 8, each time from its own state at the previous KK. For 14o, all five seeds at a given KK start from the same state: the broken-symmetry UHF determinant for K=2K=2 and the seed-0 state of the previous KK for K=4K=4 and 8, and differ only in the random rotations that initialize the added determinants. Each optimization used Adam followed by geometric direct minimization (GDM) 67 with a line search to a gradient root mean square (RMS) below 10−610^{-6}. We grouped seeds whose states coincide (infidelity below 10−610^{-6}). Although the variational energy decreases steadily with KK, the AFQMC energy does not follow this trend. The error is neither monotonic in KK nor fixed by the variational energy; in particular, for (18e, 14o) at K=8K=8 it ranges from −4.05​(6)-4.05(6) to −2.56​(8)-2.56(8) m​Eh\textup{m}E_{\textup{h}} over five states whose projected energies agree within 0.12 m​Eh\textup{m}E_{\textup{h}}. For (30e, 20o) at K=4K=4, two states 0.68 m​Eh\textup{m}E_{\textup{h}} apart in projected energy give −9.11​(14)-9.11(14) and −2.25​(12)-2.25(12) m​Eh\textup{m}E_{\textup{h}}. None of these trials brings AFQMC within chemical accuracy. This shows the limitation of compact trials optimized classically for their energy: a lower variational energy, whether from more determinants or from a lower-lying state at the same KK, does not reliably give a smaller AFQMC error, and among the classical trials considered here chemical accuracy is reached by selected-CI expansions of about 3×1053\times 10^{5} determinants or more (right column).

Figure S3.8a compares, for each LUCJ circuit and number of determinants KK, AFQMC with classical VAP-NOCI trials and QC-QMC with surrogates trained on the hardware data; panel b relates the QC-QMC error of each surrogate to its validation error relative to the noise floor.

S3.6 High-spin state of [Fe2S2(SCH3)4]2-

In contrast to the low-spin state where classical NOCI struggles, in the high-spin S=5S=5 state (Fig. S3.9), we found that classical NOCI serves as a good QMC trial. In the MS=5M_{S}=5 sector, both active spaces have at most ten open shells (2×14−18=2×20−30=102\times 14-18=2\times 20-30=10), the α\alpha shell is completely filled and a determinant with MS=5M_{S}=5 is already an S=5S=5 eigenstate, so the problem reduces to the β\beta electrons alone (1,001 and 184,756 determinants for (18e, 14o) and (30e, 20o), versus ∼4×106\sim\!4\times 10^{6} and ∼2×108\sim\!2\times 10^{8} in the singlet sector). The VAP-NOCI trials were grown by doubling KK from the UHF determinant. In contrast with the singlet, the trial energy is here a reliable guide to the AFQMC error. The variational error falls monotonically with KK, and the AFQMC error follows it. With the UHF trial, AFQMC lies +4.61​(24)+4.61(24) and +24.68​(38)+24.68(38) m​Eh\textup{m}E_{\textup{h}} above FCI; from K=4K=4 it is within chemical accuracy for both active spaces, −0.131​(12)-0.131(12) and +0.89​(7)+0.89(7) m​Eh\textup{m}E_{\textup{h}}, and from K=8K=8 within 0.06 m​Eh\textup{m}E_{\textup{h}} of FCI. We can see this only because FCI is available for both active spaces. Without a reference, one could not tell in advance whether a classical trial is reliable for a given state, and the singlet shows that the variational energy alone can mislead (Fig. S3.7). For the spin gaps (Fig. 3d and Fig. 4) we therefore treat the high-spin state exactly like the singlet, with a surrogate trained on measurements of the LUCJ circuit, and use no classical NOCI trial for the spin gap reported in the main text. Table S3.2 compares classical VAP-NOCI trials with NOCI trials learned from the hardware shadows of the (18e, 14o) high-spin circuit.

S4 Improved algorithms for matchgate shadow overlaps

Here we introduce our cubic-scaling algorithm for estimating walker overlaps from matchgate shadows, improving on a prior quartic-scaling algorithm 71. Let us first review the basic premise of classical shadows 28. Given an nn-qubit quantum state ρ\rho and a distribution of unitaries 𝒟\mathcal{D}, a randomized measurement primitive is the following procedure:

  1. 1.

    Draw a random U∼𝒟U\sim\mathcal{D};

  2. 2.

    Apply ρ↦U​ρ​U†\rho\mapsto U\rho U^{\dagger};

  3. 3.

    Measure in the computational basis, obtaining an nn-bit string bb;

  4. 4.

    Store an efficient classical description of the postmeasurement state U†​|b⟩​⟨b|​UU^{\dagger}|b\rangle\!\langle b|U.

This defines a quantum channel

ℳ:ρ↦𝔼U∼𝒟∑b∈{0,1}n⟨b|UρU†|b⟩U†|b⟩⟨b|U.\mathcal{M}:\rho\mapsto\E_{U\sim\mathcal{D}}\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\langle b|U\rho U^{\dagger}|b\rangle U^{\dagger}|b\rangle\!\langle b|U. (S4.1)

Let ℳ−1\mathcal{M}^{-1} be the inverse over the range of ℳ\mathcal{M}; for every operator O∈ran​ℳO\in\mathrm{ran}\,\mathcal{M}, by linearity and self-adjointness of ℳ\mathcal{M},

tr⁡(O​ρ)=tr⁡(ℳ−1​(O)​ℳ​(ρ))=𝔼⟨b|U​ℳ−1​(O)​U†|b⟩\tr(O\rho)=\tr(\mathcal{M}^{-1}(O)\mathcal{M}(\rho))=\E\,\langle b|U\mathcal{M}^{-1}(O)U^{\dagger}|b\rangle (S4.2)

where the expectation is over outcomes and random unitaries. Thus one has an unbiased estimate of the expectation value of OO with respect to the state ρ\rho, provided a procedure to compute the quantity ⟨b|U​ℳ−1​(O)​U†|b⟩\langle b|U\mathcal{M}^{-1}(O)U^{\dagger}|b\rangle.

S4.1 Problem statement and main theorem

Let aja_{j} be the fermionic annihilation operators and define the Majorana operators

γ2​j−1=aj+aj†,γ2​j=−i⁡(aj−aj†).\gamma_{2j-1}=a_{j}+a_{j}^{\dagger},\qquad\gamma_{2j}=-i(a_{j}-a_{j}^{\dagger}). (S4.3)

For an ordered set S={s1<⋯<s2​ℓ}S=\{s_{1}<\cdots<s_{2\ell}\}, we define Hermitian Majorana monomials γS=(−i)ℓγs1⋯γs2​ℓ\gamma_{S}=(-i)^{\ell}\gamma_{s_{1}}\cdots\gamma_{s_{2\ell}}. They form an orthogonal basis of the even operator space Γeven=span{γS:S⊆[2n],|S| even}\Gamma_{\mathrm{even}}=\spn\{\gamma_{S}:S\subseteq[2n],\ |S|\text{ even}\}; we write 𝒫2​ℓ\mathcal{P}_{2\ell} for the orthogonal projection onto this space. A matchgate circuit (fermionic Gaussian unitary) UQU_{Q} is defined by the adjoint action

UQ†​γμ​UQ=∑νQμ​ν​γν,Q∈O⁡(2​n).U_{Q}^{\dagger}\gamma_{\mu}U_{Q}=\sum_{\nu}Q_{\mu\nu}\gamma_{\nu},\qquad Q\in\mathrm{O}(2n). (S4.4)

The orthogonal group is defined as O⁡(2​n)={Q∈ℝ2​n×2​n:Q​QT=𝕀}\mathrm{O}(2n)=\{Q\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}:QQ^{\mathrm{T}}=\mathbb{I}\}. The signed permutation group B⁡(2​n)={±1}2​n⋊S⁡(2​n)\mathrm{B}(2n)=\{\pm 1\}^{2n}\rtimes\mathrm{S}(2n), where S⁡(2​n)\mathrm{S}(2n) is the symmetric group, corresponds to matchgates that are also Clifford. The matchgate shadows protocol was originally defined for determinant-11 transformations 79, and it was later shown that extending to either O⁡(2​n)\mathrm{O}(2n) or B⁡(2​n)\mathrm{B}(2n) yields the same channel and second-moment statistics 71. In fact, for Clifford matchgates, the distribution of signs is inconsequential for the measurement outcome statistics 54, 25.

Proposition S4.1.

The measurement channel for matchgate shadows over the Haar measure on O⁡(2​n)\mathrm{O}(2n) is

ℳ≔𝔼Q∼O⁡(2​n)[𝒰Q†​ℳZ​𝒰Q]=∑ℓ=0nfℓ​𝒫2​ℓ,fℓ=(nℓ)/(2​n2​ℓ),\mathcal{M}\coloneqq\E_{Q\sim\mathrm{O}(2n)}\mathopen{}\left[\mathcal{U}_{Q}^{\dagger}\mathcal{M}_{Z}\mathcal{U}_{Q}\right]\mathclose{}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{n}f_{\ell}\mathcal{P}_{2\ell},\qquad f_{\ell}=\mathopen{}\left.\binom{n}{\ell}\middle/\binom{2n}{2\ell}\right.\mathclose{}, (S4.5)

where 𝒰Q​(ρ)=UQ​ρ​UQ†\mathcal{U}_{Q}(\rho)=U_{Q}\rho U_{Q}^{\dagger} and ℳZ​(ρ)=∑b∈{0,1}n⟨b|ρ⁡|b⟩|b⟩​⟨b|\mathcal{M}_{Z}(\rho)=\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\langle b|\rho|b\rangle|b\rangle\!\langle b| denotes measurement in the computational basis. Its inverse over Γeven\Gamma_{\mathrm{even}} is ℳ−1=∑ℓfℓ−1​𝒫2​ℓ\mathcal{M}^{-1}=\sum_{\ell}f_{\ell}^{-1}\mathcal{P}_{2\ell}. This holds even when replacing O⁡(2​n)\mathrm{O}(2n) with any distribution on B⁡(2​n)\mathrm{B}(2n) such that the measure over the marginal of unsigned permutations is uniform.

This also holds for variances; it is simply a consequence of the fact that ℳZ\mathcal{M}_{Z} is invariant under conjugation by 𝒰S\mathcal{U}_{S} for any S∈diag⁡({±1}2​n)S\in\diag(\{\pm 1\}^{2n}).

The covariance matrix of a state ρ\rho is

(Cρ)μ​ν=−i2​tr⁡(ρ⁡[γμ,γν]).(C_{\rho})_{\mu\nu}=-\frac{i}{2}\tr(\rho[\gamma_{\mu},\gamma_{\nu}]). (S4.6)

In particular, for any nn-bit string b∈{0,1}nb\in\{0,1\}^{n},

C|b⟩=⨁j=1n(−1)bj​(01−10),and in particular ​C|𝟎⟩=Jn.C_{|b\rangle}=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}(-1)^{b_{j}}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\text{and in particular }C_{|\mathbf{0}\rangle}=J_{n}. (S4.7)

Here and below JkJ_{k} denotes the symplectic form: kk copies of this 2×22\times 2 block. The covariance matrix of a Gaussian-rotated state UQ​ρ​UQ†U_{Q}\rho U_{Q}^{\dagger} is Q​Cρ​QTQC_{\rho}Q^{\mathrm{T}}. In particular, for a matchgate shadow outcome (Q,b)(Q,b) (a “snapshot”) of ρ\rho, the state before channel inversion is a Gaussian state ϱ⁡(Q,b)=UQ†​|b⟩​⟨b|​UQ\varrho(Q,b)=U_{Q}^{\dagger}|b\rangle\!\langle b|U_{Q}. Thus, its covariance matrix

Cϱ⁡(Q,b)=QT​C|b⟩​QC_{\varrho(Q,b)}=Q^{\mathrm{T}}C_{|b\rangle}Q (S4.8)

is a complete description of the snapshot.

The QC-QMC overlap with an arbitrary Slater determinant |φ⟩|\varphi\rangle is given by the quantity

Xφ​(Q,b)=2​tr⁡(|φ⟩​⟨𝟎|​ℳ−1​(UQ†​|b⟩​⟨b|​UQ)),X_{\varphi}(Q,b)=2\tr\mathopen{}\left(|\varphi\rangle\!\langle\mathbf{0}|\mathcal{M}^{-1}(U_{Q}^{\dagger}|b\rangle\!\langle b|U_{Q})\right)\mathclose{}, (S4.9)

where (Q,b)(Q,b) is a snapshot of the state |𝟎⟩+|ΨT⟩2\frac{|\mathbf{0}\rangle+|\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}. By linearity, it obeys 𝔼[Xφ]=⟨ΨT|φ⟩\E[X_{\varphi}]=\langle\Psi_{T}|\varphi\rangle. The key insight of Wan et al. 71 is that Eq. S4.9 can be evaluated in polynomial time by classically processing the covariance matrix Cϱ⁡(Q,b)C_{\varrho(Q,b)}.

Before recalling their result, we establish a few conventions. For even η≤n\eta\leq n, let

W=⨁j=1η12​(1−i1i)⊕𝕀2​(n−η),S¯η=[2​n]∖{1,3,…,2​η−1}.W=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{\eta}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\\ 1&i\end{pmatrix}\ \oplus\ \mathbb{I}_{2(n-\eta)},\qquad\overline{S}_{\eta}=[2n]\setminus\{1,3,\ldots,2\eta-1\}. (S4.10)

Let 2​r=2​n−η2r=2n-\eta be the size of S¯η\overline{S}_{\eta} and ΠS¯η\Pi_{\overline{S}_{\eta}} be the 2​r×2​n2r\times 2n matrix that selects the rows given by S¯η\overline{S}_{\eta}. We parametrize Slater determinants |φ⟩≡|φ⁡(V)⟩|\varphi\rangle\equiv|\varphi(V)\rangle via

|φ(V)⟩=a~1†⋯a~η†|𝟎⟩,a~j†=∑k=1nVj​k∗ak†|\varphi(V)\rangle=\widetilde{a}_{1}^{\dagger}\cdots\widetilde{a}_{\eta}^{\dagger}|\mathbf{0}\rangle,\qquad\widetilde{a}_{j}^{\dagger}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}V_{jk}^{*}a_{k}^{\dagger} (S4.11)

where the rows of VV are orthonormal. An orthogonal completion always exists for the unspecified n−ηn-\eta rows, so we shall assume that V∈U⁡(n)V\in\mathrm{U}(n). We embed U⁡(n)↪SO⁡(2​n)\mathrm{U}(n)\hookrightarrow\mathrm{SO}(2n) as

Q~​(V)=(R11⋯R1​n⋱Rn​1⋯Rn​n)∈SO⁡(2​n),Rj​k=(Re⁡Vj​k−Im⁡Vj​kIm⁡Vj​kRe⁡Vj​k).\widetilde{Q}(V)=\begin{pmatrix}R_{11}&\cdots&R_{1n}\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ R_{n1}&\cdots&R_{nn}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathrm{SO}(2n),\qquad R_{jk}=\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}V_{jk}&-\operatorname{Im}V_{jk}\\ \operatorname{Im}V_{jk}&\operatorname{Re}V_{jk}\end{pmatrix}. (S4.12)

To any given shadow–walker pair (Cϱ,V)(C_{\varrho},V), we define the following 2​r×2​r2r\times 2r skew-symmetric matrices:

C=LCϱLTwhere L=ΠS¯ηW∗Q~(V),B=(𝕆η×η00Jn−η)\begin{split}C&=LC_{\varrho}L^{\mathrm{T}}\qquad\text{where }L=\Pi_{\overline{S}_{\eta}}W^{*}\widetilde{Q}(V),\\ B&=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{O}_{\eta\times\eta}&0\\ 0&J_{n-\eta}\end{pmatrix}\end{split} (S4.13)

where 𝕆\mathbb{O} denotes the zero matrix of a specified size. Finally, the Pfaffian of a skew-symmetric matrix A∈ℂ2​r×2​rA\in\mathbb{C}^{2r\times 2r} is

pf⁡(A)=12r​r!​∑σ∈S⁡(2​r)(−1)σ​∏j=1rAσ⁡(2​j−1),σ⁡(2​j)\pf(A)=\frac{1}{2^{r}r!}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{S}(2r)}(-1)^{\sigma}\prod_{j=1}^{r}A_{\sigma(2j-1),\sigma(2j)} (S4.14)

where S⁡(2​r)\mathrm{S}(2r) is the symmetric group and (−1)σ(-1)^{\sigma} is the parity of the permutation σ\sigma.

Proposition S4.2 (Wan et al. 71 Theorem 3).

Let |φ⟩|\varphi\rangle be an nn-mode, η\eta-fermion Slater determinant with η\eta even. For the covariance matrix CϱC_{\varrho} of a matchgate shadow snapshot, define the polynomial

q⁡(z)=iη/22r​pf⁡(B+z​C)=∑ℓ=0rqℓ​zℓq(z)=\frac{i^{\eta/2}}{2^{r}}\pf(B+zC)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{r}q_{\ell}z^{\ell} (S4.15)

where BB and CC are defined as in Eq. S4.13. Then the estimator from Eq. S4.9 obeys

Xφ=2​∑ℓ=0rfℓ−1​qℓ,X_{\varphi}=2\sum_{\ell=0}^{r}f_{\ell}^{-1}q_{\ell}, (S4.16)

and the coefficients (q0,q1,…,qr)(q_{0},q_{1},\ldots,q_{r}) can be computed with 𝒪⁡(r4)\mathcal{O}(r^{4}) arithmetic operations.

Wan et al. 71 also give strong numerical evidence that the variance of XφX_{\varphi} is asymptotically bounded by the variance of X|𝟎⟩X_{|\mathbf{0}\rangle}, the latter of which they rigorously bound as Var⁡[X|𝟎⟩]=𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n)\V[X_{|\mathbf{0}\rangle}]=\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n}\log n). While their algorithm is formally efficient, it involves degree-rr polynomial interpolation in the monomial basis, which is numerically unstable and requires 𝒪⁡(r)\mathcal{O}(r)-bit precision to stay below machine precision 38. Furthermore, their algorithm scales quartically in the linear dimension of matrices BB and CC, where 2​r≤2​n2r\leq 2n. On the other hand, the Pfaffian can be evaluated (with numerical stability) in 𝒪⁡(r3)\mathcal{O}(r^{3}) arithmetic operations 74, 60, hinting at the possibility of a cubic-time algorithm for the overlap estimator.

We introduce two such algorithms here. The first is enabled by applying a complex skew-symmetric variant of the Paige–Van Loan reduction 55, 66 to the matrix pencil (B,C)(B,C). Along with a Schur complement transformation, this reduces the Pfaffian to a determinant using a formula for certain structured block matrices 53. We then compute the polynomial coefficients qℓq_{\ell} quickly using recurrence relations for determinants of Hessenberg matrices 73. We call this method the PVL method. However, this method relies on the invertibility of a certain block of CC, which does not hold for all instances.11 1 Empirically, we have observed that such instances occur with a frequency of less than 10−610^{-6} in actual QC-QMC runs. Thus we include a second method, based on the QZ algorithm for solving generalized eigenvalue problems 45, 19. This version applies to every CC, but features a slightly larger prefactor in the r3r^{3} scaling. Appropriately, we refer to it as the GEV method. As such, we record the following result.

Theorem S4.3 (Cubic-time overlap computation).

For any skew-symmetric B,C∈ℂ2​r×2​rB,C\in\mathbb{C}^{2r\times 2r}, the polynomial coefficients of pf⁡(B+z​C)\pf(B+zC) can be computed in 𝒪⁡(r3)\mathcal{O}(r^{3}) arithmetic operations.

Note on concurrent work.

Independently of our results, Nappi et al. 51 introduced an 𝒪⁡(r3)\mathcal{O}(r^{3}) method also based on the Schur complement; as such, it also suffers the same invertibility issue as ours. Their algorithm does not perform a Hessenberg reduction; instead, it adapts the derivative-based approach in Appendix D 71. To our knowledge, our GEV method is the first algorithm to solve the problem in full generality in cubic time.

S4.2 The PVL method

The key result and algorithm describing the PVL method are as follows. We always assume that the matrices B,CB,C (and hence the polynomial q⁡(z)q(z)) are defined with respect to a given shadow–walker pair, and that the particle number η\eta is even.

Theorem S4.4 (PVL algorithm).

Given a covariance matrix CϱC_{\varrho} and Slater determinant |φ⁡(V)⟩|\varphi(V)\rangle, suppose the leading η×η\eta\times\eta block C11C_{11} of

C=(C11C12−C12TC22)C=\begin{pmatrix}C_{11}&C_{12}\\ -C_{12}^{\mathrm{T}}&C_{22}\end{pmatrix} (S4.17)

is invertible. Then Algorithm 1 returns the r+1r+1 complex coefficients of the overlap polynomial q⁡(z)q(z) in 𝒪⁡(r3)\mathcal{O}(r^{3}) arithmetic operations and 𝒪⁡(r2)\mathcal{O}(r^{2}) storage, where r=n−η/2r=n-\eta/2. Specifically, it constructs an upper Hessenberg matrix H∈ℂs×sH\in\mathbb{C}^{s\times s}, s=n−ηs=n-\eta, such that

q⁡(z)=iη/2​pf⁡(C11)2r​zη/2​det(𝕀s−z​H).q(z)=\frac{i^{\eta/2}\pf(C_{11})}{2^{r}}z^{\eta/2}\det(\mathbb{I}_{s}-zH). (S4.18)

The coefficients below degree η/2\eta/2 are necessarily zero, and if we write det(𝕀s−z​H)=∑j=0sdj​zj\det(\mathbb{I}_{s}-zH)=\sum_{j=0}^{s}d_{j}z^{j}, then the remaining coefficients are qη/2+j=iη/2​2−r​pf⁡(C11)​djq_{\eta/2+j}=i^{\eta/2}2^{-r}\pf(C_{11})d_{j}.

The rest of the section proves this result. Throughout, we set

r=n−η/2,s=n−η,κ=iη/22r.r=n-\eta/2,\qquad s=n-\eta,\qquad\kappa=\frac{i^{\eta/2}}{2^{r}}. (S4.19)

Let PsP_{s} be the 2​s×2​s2s\times 2s permutation matrix satisfying

Ps​(x1y1xsys)=(x1xsy1ys).P_{s}\begin{pmatrix}x_{1}\\ y_{1}\\ \vdots\\ x_{s}\\ y_{s}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}x_{1}\\ \vdots\\ x_{s}\\ y_{1}\\ \vdots\\ y_{s}\end{pmatrix}. (S4.20)

Its determinant is det(Ps)=ϵs=(−1)s⁡(s−1)/2\det(P_{s})=\epsilon_{s}=(-1)^{s(s-1)/2}. The 2​r×2​r2r\times 2r permutation matrix RR is then defined as R=𝕀η⊕PsR=\mathbb{I}_{\eta}\oplus P_{s}, and for the pair (B,C)(B,C) we set

B′=RBRT=(𝕆η×η00Js′),Js′=(0𝕀s−𝕀s0),C′=R​C​RT=(C11C12′−C12′TC22′).\begin{split}B^{\prime}&=RBR^{\mathrm{T}}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{O}_{\eta\times\eta}&0\\ 0&J^{\prime}_{s}\end{pmatrix},\qquad J_{s}^{\prime}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\mathbb{I}_{s}\\ -\mathbb{I}_{s}&0\end{pmatrix},\\ C^{\prime}&=RCR^{\mathrm{T}}=\begin{pmatrix}C_{11}&C_{12}^{\prime}\\ -C_{12}^{\prime\mathrm{T}}&C_{22}^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}.\end{split} (S4.21)

The blocks of C′C^{\prime} conform with the structure of B′B^{\prime}, i.e., C11∈ℂη×ηC_{11}\in\mathbb{C}^{\eta\times\eta} and C22′∈ℂ2​s×2​sC_{22}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{C}^{2s\times 2s}. Note that RR leaves the leading η×η\eta\times\eta block unchanged. The following lemma reduces the overlap polynomial to a Pfaffian variant of the characteristic polynomial 1. A subsequent reduction that we call symplectic Hessenberg further reduces this Pfaffian to an ordinary determinant of half the linear matrix dimension.

Lemma S4.5.

Suppose C11C_{11} is invertible, and define the skew Schur complement of C′C^{\prime}:

M=C22′+C12′T​C11−1​C12′.M=C_{22}^{\prime}+C_{12}^{\prime\mathrm{T}}C_{11}^{-1}C_{12}^{\prime}. (S4.22)

Then

q⁡(z)=κ​ϵs​zη/2​pf⁡(C11)​pf⁡(Js′+z​M)q(z)=\kappa\epsilon_{s}z^{\eta/2}\pf(C_{11})\pf(J_{s}^{\prime}+zM) (S4.23)

identically as a polynomial over z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C}.

Proof.

Set

T=(𝕀η0C12T​C11−1𝕀2​s).T=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{I}_{\eta}&0\\ C_{12}^{\mathrm{T}}C_{11}^{-1}&\mathbb{I}_{2s}\end{pmatrix}. (S4.24)

T⁡(B′+z​C′)​TT=T​(z​C11z​C12′−z​C12′TJs′+z​C22′)​TT=(z​C1100Js′+z​M).T(B^{\prime}+zC^{\prime})T^{\mathrm{T}}=T\begin{pmatrix}zC_{11}&zC_{12}^{\prime}\\ -zC_{12}^{\prime\mathrm{T}}&J_{s}^{\prime}+zC_{22}^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}T^{\mathrm{T}}=\begin{pmatrix}zC_{11}&0\\ 0&J_{s}^{\prime}+zM\end{pmatrix}. pf⁡(B+z​C)=pf⁡[RT​(B′+z​C′)​R]=pf⁡[(T​R)T​(z​C1100Js′+z​M)​T​R]=ϵs​zη/2​pf⁡(C11)​pf⁡(Js′+z​M).\begin{split}\pf(B+zC)&=\pf\mathopen{}\left[R^{\mathrm{T}}(B^{\prime}+zC^{\prime})R\right]\mathclose{}\\ &=\pf\mathopen{}\left[(TR)^{\mathrm{T}}\begin{pmatrix}zC_{11}&0\\ 0&J_{s}^{\prime}+zM\end{pmatrix}TR\right]\mathclose{}\\ &=\epsilon_{s}z^{\eta/2}\pf(C_{11})\pf(J_{s}^{\prime}+zM).\end{split} (S4.26)
