Note that we can solve the linear equation C11​X=C12C_{11}X=C_{12} to form M=C22+C12T​XM=C_{22}+C_{12}^{\mathrm{T}}X, rather than explicitly constructing a matrix inverse. The sign ϵs\epsilon_{s} in Eq. S4.23 is essential; in the following reduction, a second copy of the same sign will appear, thereby canceling the two.

Symplectic Hessenberg reduction.

The following reduction is the main matrix subroutine to bring pf⁡(Js′+z​M)\pf(J_{s}^{\prime}+zM) to a convenient form. It is essentially equivalent to the Paige–Van Loan reduction for Hamiltonian and skew-Hamiltonian matrices 55, 66, up to an appropriate transformation. We give a specialized treatment for our context and provide an explicit, self-contained description of the algorithm involving complex symplectic Givens rotations.

Recall that a matrix is said to be (upper) Hessenberg if it has all zero entries below the first subdiagonal.

Theorem S4.6 (Symplectic Hessenberg reduction).

For every complex skew-symmetric M∈ℂ2​s×2​sM\in\mathbb{C}^{2s\times 2s} there is a product UU of symplectic Givens rotations (Definition S4.7) such that

U​M​UT=(0−HTHZ),H∈ℂs×s​ is upper Hessenberg,Z=−ZT.UMU^{\mathrm{T}}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-H^{\mathrm{T}}\\ H&Z\end{pmatrix},\qquad H\in\mathbb{C}^{s\times s}\text{ is upper Hessenberg},\quad Z=-Z^{\mathrm{T}}. (S4.27)

Moreover, U​Js′​UT=Js′UJ_{s}^{\prime}U^{\mathrm{T}}=J_{s}^{\prime} (hence det(U)=1\det(U)=1). The reduction uses 𝒪⁡(s3)\mathcal{O}(s^{3}) arithmetic operations and 𝒪⁡(s2)\mathcal{O}(s^{2}) storage.

The procedure to compute UU is given in Algorithm 2.

We use symplectic unitary transformations UU, i.e., satisfying U​Js′​UT=Js′UJ_{s}^{\prime}U^{\mathrm{T}}=J_{s}^{\prime} and U​U†=𝕀UU^{\dagger}=\mathbb{I}. Note the distinct uses of transpose and conjugate transpose: unitary congruence A→U​A​UTA\to UAU^{\mathrm{T}} is essential to preserve skew symmetry, rather than conjugation. Our elementary rotations GG are defined as follows.

Definition S4.7 (Symplectic Givens rotations).

Consider complex Givens rotations of the form

G=(cu−u∗c),c∈ℝ,c2+|u|2=1.G=\begin{pmatrix}c&u\\ -u^{*}&c\end{pmatrix},\qquad c\in\mathbb{R},\quad c^{2}+|u|^{2}=1. (S4.28)

Given such a GG, we define two ways to embed it into the 2​s2s coordinates:

  • •

    An inter-block rotation Ginter(i)G_{\mathrm{inter}}^{(i)} applies GG on coordinates (i,s+i)(i,s+i).

  • •

    An intra-block rotation Gintra(i,j)G_{\mathrm{intra}}^{(i,j)} applies GG on coordinates (i,j)(i,j) and G∗G^{*} on coordinates (s+i,s+j)(s+i,s+j).

The transformations Ginter(i)G_{\mathrm{inter}}^{(i)} and Gintra(i,j)G_{\mathrm{intra}}^{(i,j)} are unitary and symplectic with respect to Js′J_{s}^{\prime}. Given a,b∈ℂa,b\in\mathbb{C}, the Givens rotation is chosen to map (a,b)T(a,b)^{\mathrm{T}} either to (0,v)T(0,v)^{\mathrm{T}} or to (v,0)T(v,0)^{\mathrm{T}}, where |v|2=|a|2+|b|2|v|^{2}=|a|^{2}+|b|^{2}. For example, writing w=ei⁡(arg⁡a−arg⁡b)w=e^{i(\arg a-\arg b)} and d=|a|2+|b|2d=\sqrt{|a|^{2}+|b|^{2}}, the first choice has c=|b|/dc=|b|/d, u=−w|a|/du=-w|a|/d, while the second has c=|a|/dc=|a|/d, u=w​|b|/du=w|b|/d. If both inputs vanish, we take G=𝕀2G=\mathbb{I}_{2} with an arbitrary phase choice.

Proof (of Theorem S4.6).

We prove the zero pattern by induction on jj. Before processing column jj, every earlier column k<jk<j has a zero upper half, and its lower half vanishes at rows s+is+i with i>k+1i>k+1. This is vacuous at j=1j=1.

In the first loop, we have i>ji>j. At a previous column k<jk<j, both entries mixed by Ginter(i)G_{\mathrm{inter}}^{(i)} vanish: the upper entry is in a previously zeroed column of the upper-left block, and the lower entry has i>k+1i>k+1. Thus the left multiplication preserves these entries. Right multiplication only changes columns ii and s+is+i, so it leaves columns 1,…,j1,\ldots,j unchanged. Consequently, we may zero out all entries Ai​jA_{ij} for i>ji>j without disturbing the completed columns or earlier zeros in the current column.

In the second loop, the affected upper indices (i−1,i)(i-1,i) are both greater than jj. Thus, they contain zeros in column jj after the first loop. At previous columns k<jk<j, their lower partners also vanish because i−1≥j+1>k+1i-1\geq j+1>k+1. The rotations preserve all of these zeros. Right multiplication again leaves columns 1,…,j1,\ldots,j unchanged. Processing the lower entries from bottom to top leaves only rows s+1,…,s+j+1s+1,\ldots,s+j+1 possibly nonzero in the lower half of column jj.

By skew symmetry, all the corresponding rows are also zeroed out, and the diagonal of MM is automatically zero. As such, after column s−1s-1, the remaining upper-left entry is diagonal, hence zero automatically. The lower-left block has precisely the upper Hessenberg pattern, while the lower-right block remains generally dense and skew-symmetric. Every rotation preserves Js′J_{s}^{\prime} and has determinant one, so the accumulated transformation has the claimed properties.

To bound the complexity, observe that there are s⁡(s−1)/2s(s-1)/2 inter-block rotations and (s−1)​(s−2)/2(s-1)(s-2)/2 intra-block rotations, and each congruence transformation updates a constant number of rows and columns in 𝒪⁡(s)\mathcal{O}(s) time. ∎

Corollary S4.8.

Let HH be the output of Algorithm 2. Then

pf⁡(Js′+z​M)=ϵs​det(𝕀s−z​H),\pf(J_{s}^{\prime}+zM)=\epsilon_{s}\det(\mathbb{I}_{s}-zH), (S4.29)

and hence

q⁡(z)=κ​pf⁡(C11)​zη/2​det(𝕀s−z​H).q(z)=\kappa\pf(C_{11})z^{\eta/2}\det(\mathbb{I}_{s}-zH). (S4.30)
Proof.

Since det(U)=1\det(U)=1, congruence by UU gives

pf(Js′+zM)=pf(0𝕀s−z​HTz​H−𝕀sz​Z).\pf(J_{s}^{\prime}+zM)=\pf\mathopen{}\begin{pmatrix}0&\mathbb{I}_{s}-zH^{\mathrm{T}}\\ zH-\mathbb{I}_{s}&zZ\end{pmatrix}. (S4.31)

For any square AA and skew-symmetric YY of the same size, we use the following identity for Pfaffians of block matrices (Corollary 2.4) 53:

pf(0A−ATY)=(−1)s⁡(s−1)/2det(A).\pf\mathopen{}\begin{pmatrix}0&A\\ -A^{\mathrm{T}}&Y\end{pmatrix}=(-1)^{s(s-1)/2}\det(A). (S4.32)

Applying this with A=𝕀s−z​HTA=\mathbb{I}_{s}-zH^{\mathrm{T}} proves Eq. S4.29. Substitution into Eq. S4.23 cancels the sign ϵs\epsilon_{s}, proving Eq. S4.30. ∎

Recurrence relation for Hessenberg determinants.

Given the upper Hessenberg block HH, the next subroutine returns all s+1s+1 coefficients of det(𝕀s−z​H)\det(\mathbb{I}_{s}-zH) in cubic time. We use a classic recurrence relation for Hessenberg matrices; see, for instance, Chapter 6, Eq. (57.1) of Wilkinson 73. Computing the determinant of an RR-valued Hessenberg matrix in this way costs 𝒪⁡(s2)\mathcal{O}(s^{2}) RR-operations. In our case, R=ℂ⁡[z]R=\mathbb{C}[z] of degree at most ss, which takes 𝒪⁡(s)\mathcal{O}(s) arithmetic operations per entry to manipulate.

Proposition S4.9 (Wilkinson 73 Chapter 6, Section 57).

Let H∈ℂs×sH\in\mathbb{C}^{s\times s} be upper Hessenberg, and let

p0(t)=1,pk(t)=det(t𝕀k−H1:k,1:k)for 1≤k≤s.p_{0}(t)=1,\qquad p_{k}(t)=\det(t\mathbb{I}_{k}-H_{1:k,1:k})\quad\text{for }1\leq k\leq s. (S4.33)

For k=1,…,sk=1,\ldots,s, we have the recurrence relation

pk​(t)=(t−Hk​k)​pk−1​(t)−∑i=1k−1Hi​k​(∏j=ik−1Hj+1,j)​pi−1​(t).p_{k}(t)=(t-H_{kk})p_{k-1}(t)-\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}H_{ik}\mathopen{}\left(\prod_{j=i}^{k-1}H_{j+1,j}\right)\mathclose{}p_{i-1}(t). (S4.34)
Corollary S4.10.

If we write ps​(t)=∑j=0saj​tjp_{s}(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{s}a_{j}t^{j}, then

det(𝕀s−z​H)=∑ℓ=0sas−ℓ​zℓ.\det(\mathbb{I}_{s}-zH)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{s}a_{s-\ell}z^{\ell}. (S4.35)

The coefficients aja_{j} can be computed using 𝒪⁡(s3)\mathcal{O}(s^{3}) arithmetic operations without divisions, and 𝒪⁡(s2)\mathcal{O}(s^{2}) storage.

Proof.

For z≠0z\neq 0, we have det(𝕀s−z​H)=zs​ps​(z−1)\det(\mathbb{I}_{s}-zH)=z^{s}p_{s}(z^{-1}). Reversing the coefficients proves Eq. S4.35, including at z=0z=0 by equality of polynomials. To bound the complexity, observe that to compute the recurrence, we first tabulate the products of consecutive subdiagonal entries in 𝒪⁡(s2)\mathcal{O}(s^{2}) time. Each step combines at most kk coefficient arrays of length at most k+1k+1, so its cost is 𝒪⁡(k2)\mathcal{O}(k^{2}). Summing over kk steps gives 𝒪⁡(s3)\mathcal{O}(s^{3}) time. The arrays for p0,p1,…,ps∈ℂ⁡[t]p_{0},p_{1},\ldots,p_{s}\in\mathbb{C}[t] and the subdiagonal products occupy 𝒪⁡(s2)\mathcal{O}(s^{2}) total storage. Finally, by Eq. S4.35 we do not need any divisions. ∎

This subroutine is summarized in Algorithm 3.

Putting these pieces together, we now prove the main result of the PVL method.

Proof (of Theorem S4.4).

Correctness is Eq. S4.30 followed by Eq. S4.35 and placement of the coefficients starting at degree η/2\eta/2. Let us verify the complexity. Evaluating the Pfaffian of C11C_{11} costs 𝒪⁡(η3)\mathcal{O}(\eta^{3}) arithmetic operations, and solving C11​X=C12′C_{11}X=C_{12}^{\prime} where C12′∈ℂη×2​sC_{12}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{C}^{\eta\times 2s} costs 𝒪⁡(η2​s)\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2}s). Forming C12′T​XC_{12}^{\prime\mathrm{T}}X costs 𝒪⁡(η​s2)\mathcal{O}(\eta s^{2}), and by Theorems S4.6 and S4.10, the symplectic Hessenberg reduction and the recurrence computation each cost 𝒪⁡(s3)\mathcal{O}(s^{3}); placing the resulting coefficients in the output vector costs 𝒪⁡(s)\mathcal{O}(s). Finally, all matrices and coefficient arrays have at most quadratic size. ∎

Remark S4.11 (Generality of the PVL method).

The approach presented above specializes to finding the polynomial pf⁡(B+z​C)\pf(B+zC) where BB has the particular structure B=𝕆η×η⊕Jn−ηB=\mathbb{O}_{\eta\times\eta}\oplus J_{n-\eta}. This applies more broadly: suppose instead that BB is an arbitrary skew-symmetric matrix of rank 2​r−η2r-\eta. Then there always exists an invertible matrix UU such that UT​B​U=𝕆η×η⊕Jn−ηU^{\mathrm{T}}BU=\mathbb{O}_{\eta\times\eta}\oplus J_{n-\eta} 26. The PVL algorithm can then be applied if the leading η×η\eta\times\eta block of UT​C​UU^{\mathrm{T}}CU is invertible.

S4.3 The GEV method

The PVL method crucially requires that C11C_{11} be invertible. Here we describe an 𝒪⁡(r3)\mathcal{O}(r^{3})-time algorithm which applies to any (B,C)(B,C), based on a reduction to a generalized eigenvalue problem (which in turn is solved by the QZ algorithm of Moler and Stewart) 45.

Theorem S4.12 (GEV algorithm).

Given a covariance matrix Cϱ∈ℝ2​n×2​nC_{\varrho}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n} and a Slater determinant |φ⁡(V)⟩|\varphi(V)\rangle, Algorithm 4 returns the r+1r+1 complex coefficients of the overlap polynomial q⁡(z)q(z) in 𝒪⁡(r3)\mathcal{O}(r^{3}) arithmetic operations and 𝒪⁡(r2)\mathcal{O}(r^{2}) storage, where r=n−η/2r=n-\eta/2. Specifically, it constructs upper triangular matrices T,S∈ℂ2​r×2​rT,S\in\mathbb{C}^{2r\times 2r} and computes a scalar α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C} such that

q⁡(z)=α​∏μ=1r(tμ−z​sμ),q(z)=\alpha\prod_{\mu=1}^{r}(t_{\mu}-zs_{\mu}), (S4.36)

where {(tμ,sμ):μ∈[r]}\{(t_{\mu},s_{\mu}):\mu\in[r]\} are the pairs of diagonal entries (Tj​j,Sj​j)(T_{jj},S_{jj}) at half multiplicity.

The GEV method is based on two key observations: first, that pf⁡(A)2=det(A)\pf(A)^{2}=\det(A) allows us to reduce a Pfaffian to a determinant up to a sign; and second, that B+z​CB+zC is a linear matrix pencil whose characteristic polynomial det(B+z​C)\det(B+zC) can be determined from the generalized eigenvalue equation B​v=−λ​C​vBv=-\lambda Cv.

The QZ algorithm.

First we review some basic theory of matrix pencils. Let A,BA,B be square matrices. A matrix pencil is the ray A−λ​BA-\lambda B, where λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C}. We also write a pencil as the pair (A,B)(A,B). The characteristic polynomial of (A,B)(A,B) is

p⁡(λ)=det(A−λ​B).p(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda B). (S4.37)

The pencil is called regular if p∈ℂ⁡[λ]p\in\mathbb{C}[\lambda] is not the zero polynomial, and singular otherwise.

The generalized eigenvalues of a matrix pencil are given by the set

λ⁡(A,B)={z∈ℂ:p⁡(z)=0}.\lambda(A,B)=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:p(z)=0\}. (S4.38)

The pencil (A,B)(A,B) is singular if and only if λ⁡(A,B)=ℂ\lambda(A,B)=\mathbb{C}. Otherwise, |λ⁡(A,B)|≤rank⁡(B)|\lambda(A,B)|\leq\rank(B). The generalized eigenvalues can be determined from the generalized Schur decomposition of the pencil 45, 19.

Proposition S4.13 (Generalized Schur decomposition 19 Theorem 7.7.1).

For any matrix pencil (A,B)(A,B), there exist unitary matrices Q,ZQ,Z such that

A=Q​T​Z†,B=Q​S​Z†A=QTZ^{\dagger},\qquad B=QSZ^{\dagger} (S4.39)

for upper triangular T,ST,S. If there exists some jj such that Tj​j=Sj​j=0T_{jj}=S_{jj}=0, then λ⁡(A,B)=ℂ\lambda(A,B)=\mathbb{C}. Otherwise,

λ⁡(A,B)={Tj​j/Sj​j:Sj​j≠0}.\lambda(A,B)=\{T_{jj}/S_{jj}:S_{jj}\neq 0\}. (S4.40)

There are also “infinite eigenvalues” of (A,B)(A,B), corresponding to when Sj​j=0S_{jj}=0 but Tj​j≠0T_{jj}\neq 0. These merely contribute to the characteristic polynomial as an overall scale factor, as can be seen from

p⁡(λ)=det(Q​Z†)​∏j(Tj​j−λ​Sj​j).p(\lambda)=\det(QZ^{\dagger})\prod_{j}(T_{jj}-\lambda S_{jj}). (S4.41)

The standard procedure to bring a pencil into generalized Schur form is the QZ algorithm.

Proposition S4.14 (QZ algorithm 45, 19).

The generalized Schur decomposition of an N×NN\times N matrix pencil can be determined in 𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}) arithmetic operations.

Reconstructing coefficients from roots.

Now let B,CB,C be the skew-symmetric overlap matrices from Eq. S4.13. The overall strategy of Algorithm 4 is to compute the generalized eigenvalues λ⁡(B,−C)\lambda(B,-C). This is the set of roots of the polynomial det(B+z​C)\det(B+zC), which is the square of the desired polynomial pf⁡(B+z​C)\pf(B+zC). A polynomial is equivalently specified by either its coefficients or roots, up to a nonzero scalar factor. Thus, with some clean-up (whose cost is subleading compared to the cost of the QZ algorithm), we can recover qℓq_{\ell} from the roots.

Lemma S4.15.

Suppose the pencil (B,−C)(B,-C) is regular, and that q⁡(z)q(z) has degree d≤rd\leq r. Its characteristic polynomial has 2​d2d finite roots, counted with multiplicity, each with even multiplicity. Take half the multiplicity of each finite root to form a list λ1,…,λd\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d}. For any z0z_{0} with p⁡(z0)≠0p(z_{0})\neq 0,

q⁡(z)=iη/22r​pf⁡(B+z0​C)​∏j=1dz−λjz0−λj.q(z)=\frac{i^{\eta/2}}{2^{r}}\pf(B+z_{0}C)\prod_{j=1}^{d}\frac{z-\lambda_{j}}{z_{0}-\lambda_{j}}. (S4.42)

The remaining 2​r−2​d2r-2d roots are at infinity.

Proof.

The identity pf⁡(A)2=det(A)\pf(A)^{2}=\det(A) implies that every root of det(B+z​C)\det(B+zC) has even multiplicity. Hence λ⁡(B,−C)={Tj​j/Sj​j:Sj​j≠0}\lambda(B,-C)=\{T_{jj}/S_{jj}:S_{jj}\neq 0\} inherits this multiplicity, where T,ST,S are the upper triangular matrices of the generalized Schur decomposition. As in Eq. S4.41, we can write

det(B+z​C)=α​∏j=12​d(Tj​j−z​Sj​j)=α​∏i=12​dSi​i​∏j=12​d(Tj​jSj​j−z)=α′​∏j=1d(z−λj)2,\det(B+zC)=\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{2d}(T_{jj}-zS_{jj})=\alpha\prod_{i=1}^{2d}S_{ii}\prod_{j=1}^{2d}\mathopen{}\left(\frac{T_{jj}}{S_{jj}}-z\right)\mathclose{}=\alpha^{\prime}\prod_{j=1}^{d}(z-\lambda_{j})^{2}, (S4.43)

where we have absorbed all scalar factors into α′\alpha^{\prime}. Hence pf⁡(B+z​C)=α′′​∏j=1d(z−λj)\pf(B+zC)=\alpha^{\prime\prime}\prod_{j=1}^{d}(z-\lambda_{j}) for another scalar α′′\alpha^{\prime\prime}. To determine that scalar, we simply evaluate the polynomial at some non-root z0z_{0}. ∎

Note that because (B,−C)(B,-C) is a regular pencil, there are only finitely many roots and so almost all z0∈ℂz_{0}\in\mathbb{C} are not roots. Thus one could randomly sample in a region, for example the unit disc, and obtain a valid reference point almost surely.

Remark S4.16 (Heuristic for finding non-roots).

In practice, for better numerical stability, we find z0z_{0} by a small numerical optimization heuristic. Parametrize z0=R​ei​θz_{0}=R\,e^{i\theta} for some small fixed R∼1R\sim 1. We run bounded Brent minimization on the cost function ℒ(θ)=−∑j=1dlog|Rei​θ−λj|\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\sum_{j=1}^{d}\log|R\,e^{i\theta}-\lambda_{j}| over θ∈[−π,π)\theta\in[-\pi,\pi). This returns a reasonably large value of |p⁡(R​ei​θ)||p(R\,e^{i\theta})|, which boosts numerical stability since we divide by p⁡(R​ei​θ)p(R\,e^{i\theta}). Recall that we are guaranteed that only finitely many zeros may exist on this circle, if any.

We can now prove the main result of the GEV method.

Proof (of Theorem S4.12).

If (B,−C)(B,-C) is singular, then Algorithm 4 correctly returns all zeros for the polynomial. Otherwise, the pencil is regular and so Lemma S4.15 proves correctness of reconstructing the polynomial from its roots. As noted in Remark S4.16 and the comment directly above, there are only finitely many forbidden values for z0z_{0}. The single Pfaffian evaluation fixes the overall scalar, and multiplication by iη/2​2−ri^{\eta/2}2^{-r} gives qq.

The numerical linear algebraic primitives—QZ algorithm and Pfaffian evaluation—have 𝒪⁡(r3)\mathcal{O}(r^{3}) cost. The remaining steps have at most quadratic cost:

  1. 1.

    Pairing roots can be accomplished in the worst case by enumerating and checking all r⁡(r−1)2\frac{r(r-1)}{2} pairs.

  2. 2.

    Ordinary multiplication of the factors (z−λj)(z-\lambda_{j}) costs 𝒪⁡(r2)\mathcal{O}(r^{2}) to reconstruct the polynomial coefficients, and this can be improved to 𝒪⁡(r​log2​r)\mathcal{O}(r\log^{2}r) using FFT multiplication for polynomials 69.

Finally, we only need 𝒪⁡(r2)\mathcal{O}(r^{2}) space to store the constant number of matrices throughout the computation. ∎

Remark S4.17 (Normal forms for skew-symmetric matrix pencils).

While the QZ algorithm applies to any pencil, it does not use the skew-symmetric structure of our problem. This requires operating on a matrix roughly twice the size needed and identifying the double-multiplicity roots. Thompson 62 proved the existence of a skew-symmetric Kronecker normal form, which is a pencil analog of the Jordan normal form. In principle, this affords the desired reductions; in practice, this is not an algorithmic result, and besides, the Kronecker normal form is numerically unstable (just as the Jordan normal form also is). The theory of stratification 17 gives a systematic way to probe such instabilities, but does not comport with the high throughput required of QC-QMC. Our symplectic Hessenberg reduction is therefore a possible numerically stable skew-symmetric pencil normal form, although it is not fully general, as it requires one of the matrices to be invertible.

S4.4 Fast practical runtime implementation

Here we describe some bespoke modifications to our implementation to maximize performance in practice. Although n=40n=40 qubits is large compared to prior QC-QMC experiments, each individual linear-algebraic step on matrices of size 2​n−η2n-\eta is fairly modest by modern high-performance computing standards. We find that a mixture of the skew-Schur complement representation from the PVL method and the polynomial interpolation approach from the original work 71 strikes a good balance of practical speed and precision. Note that, by virtue of using interpolation, the asymptotic cost here scales as 𝒪⁡(r4)\mathcal{O}(r^{4}); nonetheless, the smaller constant prefactors remain advantageous at the scales we probe. See Fig. S2.1 for the wall-time gains.

The key improvement that we make here is to use Fourier interpolation to mitigate numerical ill-conditioning. Recall from the proof of Lemma S4.5 that, assuming C11C_{11} is invertible, we can write

pf⁡(B+z​C)=zη/2​pf⁡(C11)​pf⁡(Js+z​M),M=C22+C12T​C11−1​C12,\pf(B+zC)=z^{\eta/2}\pf(C_{11})\pf(J_{s}+zM),\qquad M=C_{22}+C_{12}^{\mathrm{T}}C_{11}^{-1}C_{12}, (S4.44)

where, for simplicity, we do not permute the rows and columns according to PsP_{s}. Let p⁡(z)=pf⁡(Js+z​M)p(z)=\pf(J_{s}+zM). From this form, we know that p⁡(z)p(z) has degree exactly s=r−η/2s=r-\eta/2, and we can perform polynomial interpolation by evaluating p⁡(z)p(z) at s+1s+1 points. To ameliorate the poor conditioning of polynomial interpolation in the monomial basis, we can work in the Fourier basis. The idea is that we do not need to compute the polynomial coefficients necessarily in the monomial basis; any basis suffices as long as we transform the coefficients fℓ−1f_{\ell}^{-1} in the same way.

Let ω=e2​π​i/(s+1)\omega=e^{2\pi i/(s+1)} be a root of unity and choose nodes zj=R​ωjz_{j}=R\,\omega^{j} for some radius R>0R>0 (we choose R=1R=1 in our implementation). If p⁡(z)=∑k=0sak​zkp(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{s}a_{k}z^{k} in the monomial basis, then by Fourier orthogonality we have

ak=1Rk​(s+1)​∑j=0sp⁡(zj)​ω−j​k.a_{k}=\frac{1}{R^{k}(s+1)}\sum_{j=0}^{s}p(z_{j})\omega^{-jk}. (S4.45)

Thus, for any fixed coefficients bkb_{k}, we have

∑k=0sbk​ak=∑j=0swj​p​(zj),where ​wj=1s+1​∑k=0sbk​R−k​ω−j​k.\sum_{k=0}^{s}b_{k}a_{k}=\sum_{j=0}^{s}w_{j}p(z_{j}),\qquad\text{where }w_{j}=\frac{1}{s+1}\sum_{k=0}^{s}b_{k}R^{-k}\omega^{-jk}. (S4.46)

Indeed, our goal is to compute the contraction (recall Eqs. S4.16 and S4.4)

X=2​κ​pf⁡(C11)​∑k=0sfk+η/2−1​ak,X=2\kappa\pf(C_{11})\sum_{k=0}^{s}f_{k+\eta/2}^{-1}a_{k}, (S4.47)

so taking bk=fk+η/2−1b_{k}=f_{k+\eta/2}^{-1} we can precompute all the new weights wjw_{j}, applicable to every shadow and every walker. Technically, we precompute the modified weights w~j\widetilde{w}_{j} defined below: substituting the expression for aka_{k} from Eq. S4.45, we get

X=pf(C11)∑j=0sw~jpf(Js+zjM),where w~j=2​κs+1∑k=0sfk+η/2−1R−ke−2πijk/(s+1).X=\pf(C_{11})\sum_{j=0}^{s}\widetilde{w}_{j}\pf(J_{s}+z_{j}M),\qquad\text{where }\widetilde{w}_{j}=\frac{2\kappa}{s+1}\sum_{k=0}^{s}f_{k+\eta/2}^{-1}R^{-k}e^{-2\pi ijk/(s+1)}. (S4.48)

We then evaluate the Pfaffian at the s+1s+1 roots of unity zjz_{j}, each costing 𝒪⁡(s3)\mathcal{O}(s^{3}) operations. Unlike naive interpolation (say, with Chebyshev nodes), this Fourier transform has an 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) condition number.

Note that this approach requires an invertible C11C_{11}, just as in the PVL method. In the rare cases where the block is singular, we also fall back to evaluating the full pencil directly.

S4.5 Analytical derivatives

The force bias and local energy in Eq. (S2.11) require first and second derivatives of the overlap with respect to the walker orbitals. We evaluate these derivatives using an alternative factorization of the polynomial q⁡(z)q(z) from Eq. (S4.15), which allows us to separate the snapshot dependence from the walkers. This approach also does not require an invertible C11C_{11}. As in the previous subsection, we use a fast numerical implementation of interpolation rather than a formally cubic-scaling primitive.

Alternative factorization of the polynomial.

To match the convention of Section S2.1, let Φ∈ℂn×η\Phi\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times\eta} be the walker coefficients, corresponding to the first η\eta rows of V†V^{\dagger} as defined in Eq. (S4.11). For each snapshot covariance matrix CϱC_{\varrho}, define the following skew-symmetric matrix:

F⁡(z)=−i⁡[𝕀n⊗(1−i)]​(Jn+z​Cϱ)−1​[𝕀n⊗(1−i)]T∈ℂn×n.F(z)=-i\mathopen{}\left[\mathbb{I}_{n}\otimes\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\end{pmatrix}\right]\mathclose{}(J_{n}+zC_{\varrho})^{-1}\mathopen{}\left[\mathbb{I}_{n}\otimes\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\end{pmatrix}\right]^{\mathrm{T}}\mathclose{}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}. (S4.49)

Note that because JnJ_{n} is full rank, (Jn+z​Cϱ)−1(J_{n}+zC_{\varrho})^{-1} exists everywhere except for finitely many values of zz, so throughout we may assume that zz is outside of those singularities. Equivalently, one may treat F⁡(z)F(z) as a fixed matrix whose entries are taken from the field of rational functions. The rectangular matrix 𝕀n⊗(1−i)\mathbb{I}_{n}\otimes(\begin{matrix}1&-i\end{matrix}) simply applies the same row (1,−i)(1,-i) to every canonical Majorana pair (2​j−1,2​j)(2j-1,2j) in the covariance matrix space. These are the creation-operator rows from WW in Eq. (S4.10), without the 1/21/\sqrt{2} normalization. In particular, F⁡(z)F(z) depends on the snapshot CϱC_{\varrho} and polynomial indeterminate zz, while all walker dependence will enter separately through Φ\Phi.

To derive the factorization, we will use the following identity for any invertible skew-symmetric matrix AA (Theorem 2.6 of ref. 32):

pf⁡(A⁡[X¯])=(−1)∑j∈Xj​pf⁡(A)​pf​(A−1​[X]),X⊆[2​n],\pf\mathopen{}\left(A[\overline{X}]\right)\mathclose{}=(-1)^{\sum_{j\in X}j}\,\pf(A)\pf\mathopen{}\left(A^{-1}[X]\right)\mathclose{},\qquad X\subseteq[2n], (S4.50)

where A⁡[X]A[X] is the principal submatrix of AA given by the rows and columns indexed by XX. In our case, X=SηX=S_{\eta} is the complement of S¯η\overline{S}_{\eta} and ∑j∈Xj=1+3+⋯+(2​η−1)=η2\sum_{j\in X}j=1+3+\cdots+(2\eta-1)=\eta^{2} is always even. Now introduce the pencil

A⁡(z)=W∗​Q~​(V)​(Jn+z​Cϱ)​Q~​(V)T​W†,A(z)=W^{*}\widetilde{Q}(V)(J_{n}+zC_{\varrho})\widetilde{Q}(V)^{\mathrm{T}}W^{\dagger}, (S4.51)

which recovers A⁡(z)​[S¯η]=B+z​CA(z)[\overline{S}_{\eta}]=B+zC. Using Eq. S4.50, we have

pf⁡(B+z​C)=pf⁡(A⁡(z))​pf​(A​(z)−1​[Sη]).\pf(B+zC)=\pf(A(z))\pf\mathopen{}\left(A(z)^{-1}[S_{\eta}]\right)\mathclose{}. (S4.52)

We will evaluate these two factors separately.

For the first factor, we use the classic identity pf⁡(P​M​PT)=det(P)​pf⁡(M)\pf(PMP^{\mathrm{T}})=\det(P)\pf(M). In Eq. (S4.51), this is P=W∗​Q~​(V)P=W^{*}\widetilde{Q}(V) and M=Jn+z​CϱM=J_{n}+zC_{\varrho}. Each of the η\eta nontrivial 2×22\times 2 blocks of W∗W^{*} has determinant −i-i, and detQ~​(V)=1\det\widetilde{Q}(V)=1. Thus

pf⁡(A⁡(z))=det(W∗​Q~​(V))​pf⁡(Jn+z​Cϱ)=(−i)η​pf⁡(Jn+z​Cϱ).\pf(A(z))=\det(W^{*}\widetilde{Q}(V))\pf(J_{n}+zC_{\varrho})=(-i)^{\eta}\pf(J_{n}+zC_{\varrho}). (S4.53)

For the second factor, first invert the full matrix in Eq. (S4.51). Since WW is unitary and Q~​(V)\widetilde{Q}(V) is real orthogonal, the inverse is

A​(z)−1=W​Q~​(V)​(Jn+z​Cϱ)−1​Q~​(V)T​WT.A(z)^{-1}=W\widetilde{Q}(V)(J_{n}+zC_{\varrho})^{-1}\widetilde{Q}(V)^{\mathrm{T}}W^{\mathrm{T}}. (S4.54)

Let ΠSη\Pi_{S_{\eta}} be the analogue of ΠS¯η\Pi_{\overline{S}_{\eta}}. The rows of W​Q~​(V)W\widetilde{Q}(V) selected by ΠSη\Pi_{S_{\eta}} can be computed one block at a time: for row jj and column kk, the block multiplication is

12​(1−i)​(Re⁡Vj​k−Im⁡Vj​kIm⁡Vj​kRe⁡Vj​k)=Vj​k∗2​(1−i)=Φk​j2​(1−i).\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}V_{jk}&-\operatorname{Im}V_{jk}\\ \operatorname{Im}V_{jk}&\operatorname{Re}V_{jk}\end{pmatrix}=\frac{V_{jk}^{*}}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\end{pmatrix}=\frac{\Phi_{kj}}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\end{pmatrix}. (S4.55)

Putting these blocks together gives

ΠSη​W​Q~​(V)=12​ΦT​[𝕀n⊗(1−i)].\Pi_{S_{\eta}}W\widetilde{Q}(V)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\Phi^{\mathrm{T}}\mathopen{}\left[\mathbb{I}_{n}\otimes\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\end{pmatrix}\right]\mathclose{}. (S4.56)

Extracting rows and columns SηS_{\eta} in Eq. (S4.54) therefore yields

A​(z)−1​[Sη]\displaystyle A(z)^{-1}[S_{\eta}] =(ΠSη​W​Q~​(V))​(Jn+z​Cϱ)−1​(ΠSη​W​Q~​(V))T\displaystyle=(\Pi_{S_{\eta}}W\widetilde{Q}(V))(J_{n}+zC_{\varrho})^{-1}(\Pi_{S_{\eta}}W\widetilde{Q}(V))^{\mathrm{T}}

Derivative formulas.

For a fixed snapshot CϱC_{\varrho} and node jj, consider the walker evolved by some one-body transformation generated by H∈ℂn×nH\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}: Sj​(t)=(et​H​Φ)T​Fj​(et​H​Φ)S_{j}(t)=(e^{tH}\Phi)^{\mathrm{T}}F_{j}(e^{tH}\Phi). The derivatives to compute the force bias and local energy are with respect to this perturbation in tt. We can compute the derivatives of Sj​(t)S_{j}(t) using the product rule. Henceforth, all derivatives are evaluated at t=0t=0 and we omit the explicit dependence on tt for notational brevity:

Assume first that SjS_{j} is invertible. Jacobi’s formula for the derivative of the Pfaffian is

∂tpf⁡(Sj)\displaystyle\partial_{t}\pf(S_{j}) =12​pf⁡(Sj)​tr⁡(Sj−1​∂tSj)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\pf(S_{j})\tr(S_{j}^{-1}\partial_{t}S_{j})

Substituting the expressions for ∂tSj\partial_{t}S_{j} and ∂tpf⁡(Sj)\partial_{t}\pf(S_{j}) and expanding yields

Assembling the estimates with reuse.

These formulas allow the Hamiltonian contractions to be shared across snapshots. For the first derivative, observe that

∂tXφ=∑j=0scj​pf⁡(Sj)​tr⁡(Sj−1​ΦT​Fj​H​Φ)=tr⁡[H​Φ​∑j=0scj​pf⁡(Sj)​Sj−1​ΦT​Fj].\partial_{t}X_{\varphi}=\sum_{j=0}^{s}c_{j}\pf(S_{j})\tr(S_{j}^{-1}\Phi^{\mathrm{T}}F_{j}H\Phi)=\tr\mathopen{}\left[H\Phi\sum_{j=0}^{s}c_{j}\pf(S_{j})S_{j}^{-1}\Phi^{\mathrm{T}}F_{j}\right]\mathclose{}. (S4.72)

Thus we can sum over the nodes and snapshots before contracting with HH. Let an overline denote the average over the measured snapshots, and define

G=∑j=0scj​pf⁡(Sj)​Sj−1​ΦT​Fj¯∈ℂη×n.G=\overline{\sum_{j=0}^{s}c_{j}\pf(S_{j})S_{j}^{-1}\Phi^{\mathrm{T}}F_{j}}\in\mathbb{C}^{\eta\times n}. (S4.73)

The averaged first derivative is then

∂tXφ¯=tr⁡(H​Φ​G).\overline{\partial_{t}X_{\varphi}}=\tr(H\Phi G). (S4.74)

For each walker, we form Φ​G\Phi G once and contract it with the NγN_{\gamma} Cholesky vectors LγL_{\gamma}, which costs 𝒪⁡(Nγ​n2)\mathcal{O}(N_{\gamma}n^{2}) operations. With vγ=i​Lγv_{\gamma}=iL_{\gamma}, the force bias and local energy in Eq. (S2.11) become

x¯γ\displaystyle\bar{x}_{\gamma} =−i​Δ​τ​tr⁡(Lγ​Φ​G)Xφ¯,\displaystyle=-i\sqrt{\Delta\tau}\,\frac{\tr(L_{\gamma}\Phi G)}{\overline{X_{\varphi}}}, (S4.75)
EL\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{L}} =Ecore+tr⁡(v0​Φ​G)Xφ¯+12​Xφ¯​∑γ∂t2Xφ¯|H=Lγ.\displaystyle=E_{\mathrm{core}}+\frac{\tr(v_{0}\Phi G)}{\overline{X_{\varphi}}}+\frac{1}{2\overline{X_{\varphi}}}\sum_{\gamma}\left.\overline{\partial_{t}^{2}X_{\varphi}}\right|_{H=L_{\gamma}}. (S4.76)

The second-derivative term has a plus sign because vγ=i​Lγv_{\gamma}=iL_{\gamma}. We average both the numerator and denominator over snapshots separately before taking their ratio. It remains to show how to evaluate ∂t2Xφ¯\overline{\partial_{t}^{2}X_{\varphi}} efficiently.

The first four terms in the second derivative, Eq. (S4.71), are quadratic in H​ΦH\Phi. Setting H=LγH=L_{\gamma}, we can therefore collect the sum over γ\gamma by defining the array

Ωp​a,q​b=∑γ(Lγ​Φ)p​a​(Lγ​Φ)q​b,p,q∈[n],a,b∈[η].\Omega_{pa,qb}=\sum_{\gamma}(L_{\gamma}\Phi)_{pa}(L_{\gamma}\Phi)_{qb},\qquad p,q\in[n],\quad a,b\in[\eta]. (S4.77)

For example, the square of the trace in the first term gives

∑γ[tr⁡(Sj−1​ΦT​Fj​Lγ​Φ)]2=∑p,q=1n∑a,b=1ηΩp​a,q​b​(Sj−1​ΦT​Fj)a​p​(Sj−1​ΦT​Fj)b​q.\sum_{\gamma}[\tr(S_{j}^{-1}\Phi^{\mathrm{T}}F_{j}L_{\gamma}\Phi)]^{2}=\sum_{p,q=1}^{n}\sum_{a,b=1}^{\eta}\Omega_{pa,qb}(S_{j}^{-1}\Phi^{\mathrm{T}}F_{j})_{ap}(S_{j}^{-1}\Phi^{\mathrm{T}}F_{j})_{bq}. (S4.78)

Expanding the other three traces in the same way, and using FjT=−FjF_{j}^{\mathrm{T}}=-F_{j} and (Sj−1)T=−Sj−1(S_{j}^{-1})^{\mathrm{T}}=-S_{j}^{-1}, gives the full sum

∑γ∂t2pf⁡(Sj)|H=Lγ\displaystyle\sum_{\gamma}\left.\partial_{t}^{2}\pf(S_{j})\right|_{H=L_{\gamma}} =pf(Sj){∑p,q=1n∑a,b=1ηΩp​a,q​b[(Sj−1ΦTFj)a​p(Sj−1ΦTFj)b​q\displaystyle=\pf(S_{j})\Biggl\{\sum_{p,q=1}^{n}\sum_{a,b=1}^{\eta}\Omega_{pa,qb}\Bigl[(S_{j}^{-1}\Phi^{\mathrm{T}}F_{j})_{ap}(S_{j}^{-1}\Phi^{\mathrm{T}}F_{j})_{bq} (S4.79)
−(Sj−1​ΦT​Fj)b​p​(Sj−1​ΦT​Fj)a​q\displaystyle-(S_{j}^{-1}\Phi^{\mathrm{T}}F_{j})_{bp}(S_{j}^{-1}\Phi^{\mathrm{T}}F_{j})_{aq}
+(FjΦSj−1ΦTFj−Fj)p​q(Sj−1)a​b]\displaystyle+(F_{j}\Phi S_{j}^{-1}\Phi^{\mathrm{T}}F_{j}-F_{j})_{pq}(S_{j}^{-1})_{ab}\Bigr]
+tr[Sj−1ΦTFj(∑γLγ2)Φ]}.\displaystyle+\tr\!\left[S_{j}^{-1}\Phi^{\mathrm{T}}F_{j}\left(\sum_{\gamma}L_{\gamma}^{2}\right)\Phi\right]\Biggr\}.

The last trace follows by summing the H2​ΦH^{2}\Phi term separately. Multiplying this expression by cjc_{j}, summing over nodes j=0,1,…,sj=0,1,\ldots,s, and averaging over snapshots gives the second-derivative term in ELE_{\mathrm{L}}.

The array Ω\Omega has n2​η2n^{2}\eta^{2} entries and depends only on the walker and the Cholesky vectors. It costs 𝒪⁡(Nγ​n2​η2)\mathcal{O}(N_{\gamma}n^{2}\eta^{2}) operations to form and can be reused for every snapshot for a fixed walker Φ\Phi. The matrix ∑γLγ2\sum_{\gamma}L_{\gamma}^{2} depends only on the Hamiltonian, so we can precompute it once and apply it to each walker Φ\Phi before processing the snapshots. Thus the contractions in Eq. (S4.79) cost 𝒪⁡(n2​η2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}\eta^{2}) per walker–snapshot pair and node, independently of NγN_{\gamma}.

Handling singularities.

Finally, we must handle cases where SjS_{j} is singular or its inverse is numerically unstable. The Pfaffian is a polynomial in the matrix entries, so its derivatives exist even when SjS_{j} is singular. Likewise, the entries of pf⁡(Sj)​Sj−1\pf(S_{j})S_{j}^{-1} are (signed) Pfaffians of smaller principal submatrices, and therefore analytically extend to polynomials even where the inverse itself is undefined.

We evaluate these polynomials by shifting the matrix to nonsingular values. Choose some fixed invertible skew-symmetric matrix Δ\Delta and replace

Sj​(t)↦Sj​(t)+ϵ​Δ.S_{j}(t)\mapsto S_{j}(t)+\epsilon\Delta. (S4.80)

The shift is independent of tt, so ∂tSj\partial_{t}S_{j} and ∂t2Sj\partial_{t}^{2}S_{j} remain unchanged. Observe that the Pfaffian, its first two tt-derivatives, and pf⁡(Sj+ϵ​Δ)​(Sj+ϵ​Δ)−1​ΦT​Fj\pf(S_{j}+\epsilon\Delta)(S_{j}+\epsilon\Delta)^{-1}\Phi^{\mathrm{T}}F_{j} are all polynomials in ϵ\epsilon of degree at most η/2\eta/2. Thus we can choose η/2+1\eta/2+1 shifts on a circle centered at zero,

ϵk=ϵ0e2​π​i​k/(η/2+1),k=0,…,η/2,\epsilon_{k}=\epsilon_{0}e^{2\pi ik/(\eta/2+1)},\qquad k=0,\ldots,\eta/2, (S4.81)

with ϵ0≠0\epsilon_{0}\neq 0 chosen so that the shifted matrices are invertible. For each power appearing in these polynomials, we have the convenient identity

1η/2+1​∑k=0η/2ϵkd={1,d=0,0,1≤d≤η/2.\frac{1}{\eta/2+1}\sum_{k=0}^{\eta/2}\epsilon_{k}^{d}=\begin{cases}1,&d=0,\\ 0,&1\leq d\leq\eta/2.\end{cases} (S4.82)

Averaging the shifted values therefore allows us to extract the constant term, which is the desired value at ϵ=0\epsilon=0. The same averaging is applied to the Pfaffian and both derivatives.

As an implementation note, we use this procedure when SjS_{j} is exactly singular, or obeys the heuristic conditioning estimate

maxa​b⁡|(Sj)a​b|×maxa​b⁡|(Sj−1)a​b|>1010.\max_{ab}|(S_{j})_{ab}|\times\max_{ab}|(S_{j}^{-1})_{ab}|>10^{10}. (S4.83)

Using AMD GPUs, we evaluate the Pfaffian, matrix inverses, and “small” matrix products (i.e., smaller than the size of Ω\Omega) in a fused kernel. Meanwhile, the contractions with Ω\Omega use batched matrix products. Supplementary Fig. S2.1 compares the implementation described here with automatic differentiation of the same estimator (one reverse pass for the force bias and one second-order pass per Cholesky vector for the local energy), showing a speedup of up to 80×80\times and agreement to within 5×10−155\times 10^{-15}.

S5 Improved matchgate circuit implementations

S5.1 Optimized compilation of Clifford matchgate shadows

Let B⁡(2​n)\mathrm{B}(2n) be the group of signed permutation matrices. We present a new procedure to compile the Clifford matchgate circuit implementing the transformation Q∈B⁡(2​n)Q\in\mathrm{B}(2n), on a one-dimensional geometry of qubits. This has improved gate count and circuit depth compared to prior state-of-the-art 78 when restricted to signed permutations, which was implemented in previous QC-QMC experiments 80. We display a spin-blocked example (i.e., running the same algorithm for two independently drawn permutations; see Section S5.2) in Fig. S1.3.

Theorem S5.1 (Clifford matchgate compilation for shadows).

Let n≥2n\geq 2. Given a permutation π0∈S⁡(2​n)\pi_{0}\in\mathrm{S}(2n), Algorithm 5 runs in 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) classical time and outputs a circuit

U=Vpm​qm⋯Vp1​q1,where Vp​q=exp(−π4γpγq),U=V_{p_{m}q_{m}}\cdots V_{p_{1}q_{1}},\qquad\text{where }V_{pq}=\exp\mathopen{}\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\gamma_{p}\gamma_{q}\right)\mathclose{}, (S5.1)

together with a new permutation π\pi and signs s∈{±1}2​ns\in\{\pm 1\}^{2n} such that U†​γj​U=sj​γπ⁡(j)U^{\dagger}\gamma_{j}U=s_{j}\gamma_{\pi(j)}. Here π\pi defines the same measurement basis as π0\pi_{0}, and it is obtained by ordering the pairs of π0\pi_{0} as in Algorithm 6. Each pair (pk,qk)(p_{k},q_{k}) belongs to either one qubit or two neighboring qubits on a one-dimensional line. The total Vp​qV_{pq} count obeys

m≤inv⁡(π)≤n⁡(n−1),m\leq\inv(\pi)\leq n(n-1), (S5.2)

with two-qubit CZ\mathrm{CZ} depth at most 2​n2n, and total circuit depth at most 4​n+14n+1. Moreover, for a uniformly random input π0\pi_{0}, the expected number of CZ\mathrm{CZ} gates, denoted NCZN_{\mathrm{CZ}}, satisfies

𝔼[NCZ]≤𝔼[m]≤n⁡(n−1)2.\E[N_{\mathrm{CZ}}]\leq\E[m]\leq\frac{n(n-1)}{2}. (S5.3)

Each Vp​qV_{pq} involving two qubits requires one CZ\mathrm{CZ} and at most four single-qubit Clifford gates.

The signs ss are recorded only for postprocessing (e.g., to compute QT​Cϱ​QQ^{\mathrm{T}}C_{\varrho}Q in the shadow-inversion step). They are a consequence of the fact that we only input an unsigned permutation π0\pi_{0}, which compiles to some circuit that implements a signed permutation (π,s)(\pi,s) whose measurement basis is equivalent to that of π0\pi_{0}, up to reordering the bits.

Compared to prior designs that adopt the continuous O⁡(2​n)\mathrm{O}(2n) compilation algorithm, our gate savings arise because we are promised a discrete Majorana permutation. The main ingredients for our improvement are:

  • •

    Discrete block synthesis. A general 4×44\times 4 orthogonal block uses six Givens rotations 78. For a permutation, the primitive 𝖲𝗈𝗋𝗍𝖥𝗈𝗎𝗋\mathsf{SortFour} produces at most three Majorana swaps, at most two of which involve two-qubit gates (Lemma S5.6).

  • •

    Direct Clifford quadratic gates. We allow all six Majorana pairs within two neighboring qubits, including the Y​XYX, X​YXY, and Y​YYY generators, in addition to the commonly used X​XXX and ZZ matchgate generators. Each cross-qubit exponential is compiled directly with one CZ\mathrm{CZ} (Eq. S5.13), rather than two CZ\mathrm{CZ} gates needed for a generic matchgate.

  • •

    Ordering the measured pairs. We employ the perfect matching pair reduction (𝖱𝖾𝖽𝗎𝖼𝖾𝖯𝖺𝗂𝗋𝗌\mathsf{ReducePairs}) of Heyraud et al. 25: order each pair (π0​(2​j−1),π0​(2​j))(\pi_{0}(2j-1),\pi_{0}(2j)) and then order the pairs by their first entries. This reduces the inversion number inv⁡(π)\inv(\pi) before compilation while preserving the shadow measurement basis (Proposition S5.5).

  • •

    Classical sign tracking. We track the signs generated by the sequence of swaps and apply them in classical postprocessing rather than implementing them as quantum gates. It was previously established that these signs do not affect the shadow measurement channel 79, 54, 25, so for matchgate shadows we only need to generate a uniformly random unsigned permutation π0∈S⁡(2​n)\pi_{0}\in\mathrm{S}(2n).

Remark S5.2 (Complete Clifford matchgate circuit compilation).

Our protocol is streamlined for matchgate shadows and the invariance of the measurements; if instead one wants to compile the matchgate circuit itself corresponding to Dt​Pπ0∈B⁡(2​n)D_{t}P_{\pi_{0}}\in\mathrm{B}(2n), then one modifies Algorithm 5 by skipping 𝖱𝖾𝖽𝗎𝖼𝖾𝖯𝖺𝗂𝗋𝗌\mathsf{ReducePairs} and applying a single layer of Pauli gates at the end that implements the signs Dt​sD_{ts} according to Supplemental Note 4, Eq. (127) 78.

We now explain the correctness and compiled circuit size of our construction.

Conventions and elementary Majorana swaps.

We work in the following Jordan–Wigner convention

γ2​j−1=Z1⋯Zj−1Xj,γ2​j=Z1⋯Zj−1Yj,j=1,…,n.\gamma_{2j-1}=Z_{1}\cdots Z_{j-1}X_{j},\qquad\gamma_{2j}=Z_{1}\cdots Z_{j-1}Y_{j},\qquad j=1,\ldots,n. (S5.4)

Since B⁡(2​n)={±1}2​n⋊S⁡(2​n)\mathrm{B}(2n)=\{\pm 1\}^{2n}\rtimes\mathrm{S}(2n), every element Q∈B⁡(2​n)Q\in\mathrm{B}(2n) can be decomposed into permutation-and-sign form: there exist π∈S⁡(2​n)\pi\in\mathrm{S}(2n) and s∈{±1}2​ns\in\{\pm 1\}^{2n} such that

Q=DsPπ,where (Pπ)j​k=δk,π⁡(j),andDs=diag(s).Q=D_{s}P_{\pi},\qquad\text{where }(P_{\pi})_{jk}=\delta_{k,\pi(j)},\quad\text{and}\quad D_{s}=\diag(s). (S5.5)

In practice, we represent π=(π⁡(1),…,π⁡(2​n))\pi=(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(2n)) as an array that records the nonzero column in each row.

For p<qp<q, define the Majorana swap gate

Vp​q=exp⁡(−π4​γp​γq)V_{pq}=\exp\mathopen{}\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\gamma_{p}\gamma_{q}\right)\mathclose{} (S5.6)

which has the B⁡(2​n)\mathrm{B}(2n)-action (0−110)\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix} between Majoranas γp\gamma_{p} and γq\gamma_{q}, and acts trivially on the rest:

Vp​q†​γp​Vp​q=−γq,Vp​q†​γq​Vp​q=γp.V_{pq}^{\dagger}\gamma_{p}V_{pq}=-\gamma_{q},\qquad V_{pq}^{\dagger}\gamma_{q}V_{pq}=\gamma_{p}. (S5.7)

Note that this signed permutation has determinant 11. We record two useful lemmas for our circuit construction.

Lemma S5.3 (Nearest-neighbor Majorana swap gates).

A swap of two Majoranas in the set {2​j−1,2​j,2​j+1,2​j+2}\{2j-1,2j,2j+1,2j+2\} can be implemented, up to a known sign, by a Clifford circuit on qubits j,j+1j,j+1. We can implement each primitive swap with at most one CZ\mathrm{CZ} gate and four single-qubit Clifford gates. In the case of either (2​j−1,2​j)(2j-1,2j) or (2​j+1,2​j+2)(2j+1,2j+2), the unitary is simply a phase gate SS.

Proof.

Write Vp​q=exp(−iπPp​q/4)V_{pq}=\exp(-i\pi P_{pq}/4) where Pp​q=−i​γp​γqP_{pq}=-i\gamma_{p}\gamma_{q}. The six cases are

(p−2​j+1,q−2​j+1)(0,1)(2,3)(1,2)(0,2)(1,3)(0,3)Pp​qZjZj+1Xj​Xj+1−Yj​Xj+1Xj​Yj+1−Yj​Yj+1.\begin{array}[]{c|cccccc}(p-2j+1,q-2j+1)&(0,1)&(2,3)&(1,2)&(0,2)&(1,3)&(0,3)\\ \hline\cr P_{pq}&Z_{j}&Z_{j+1}&X_{j}X_{j+1}&-Y_{j}X_{j+1}&X_{j}Y_{j+1}&-Y_{j}Y_{j+1}.\end{array} (S5.8)

The first two give a phase gate SS. Each remaining Pauli can be mapped to ±Zj​Zj+1\pm Z_{j}Z_{j+1} by single-qubit Clifford gates. Since exp(−iπZjZj+1/4)\exp(-i\pi Z_{j}Z_{j+1}/4) equals (Sj​Sj+1)​CZj,j+1(S_{j}S_{j+1})\mathrm{CZ}_{j,j+1} up to global phase, we only need one CZ\mathrm{CZ}. ∎

Lemma S5.4 (Updating signs).

Suppose a Clifford matchgate circuit UU currently implements Ds​PD_{s}P. The updated circuit Vp​q​UV_{pq}U implements Ds′​Tp​q​PD_{s^{\prime}}T_{pq}P, where

sj′={−sqj=p,spj=q,sjelse.s^{\prime}_{j}=\begin{cases}-s_{q}&j=p,\\ \phantom{-}s_{p}&j=q,\\ \phantom{-}s_{j}&\text{else}.\end{cases} (S5.9)

The matrix Tp​q∈B⁡(2​n)T_{pq}\in\mathrm{B}(2n) is the unsigned transposition that maps p↔qp\leftrightarrow q.

Proof.

Let D(p)=diag⁡(1,…,1,−1,1,…,1)D^{(p)}=\diag(1,\ldots,1,-1,1,\ldots,1) with the −1-1 in the ppth entry. The primitive Vp​qV_{pq} implements Rp​q=D(p)​Tp​qR_{pq}=D^{(p)}T_{pq}. Hence Vp​q​UV_{pq}U implements

Rp​q​(Ds​P)=D(p)​(Tp​q​Ds​Tp​q)​(Tp​q​P).R_{pq}(D_{s}P)=D^{(p)}(T_{pq}D_{s}T_{pq})(T_{pq}P). (S5.10)

Conjugation by Tp​qT_{pq} exchanges the two entries of ss, after which D(p)D^{(p)} flips the entry at pp. ∎

Ordering the measured pairs.

Before sorting, the shadow generator applies the pair reduction of Algorithm 1 25, which exploits the freedom to relabel the outcomes of computational basis measurements. For a permutation π0\pi_{0}, the measured Majorana pairs are (π0​(2​j−1),π0​(2​j))(\pi_{0}(2j-1),\pi_{0}(2j)), for j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n. We record the pair-ordering reduction in Algorithm 6, which first orders each pair internally, then orders the pairs by their first entries. The resulting permutation π\pi gives an equivalent measurement basis to π0\pi_{0}, except with a minimized inversion number (which affects the gate count when compiled to a one-dimensional line of qubits).

It was previously shown that this pair reduction yields an equivalent measurement basis while improving the permutation’s complexity.

Proposition S5.5 (Pair ordering 25).

Algorithm 6 preserves the measurement basis up to outcome labels and satisfies inv⁡(π)≤inv⁡(π0)\inv(\pi)\leq\inv(\pi_{0}). Hence, for uniform π0\pi_{0}, the matchgate shadow channel and variances are preserved.

Sorting four Majoranas at a time.

Our construction uses the same grouping of four Majoranas per two neighboring qubits, as in previous work 78. The additional promise that QQ is a signed permutation lets us replace their continuous block elimination by instead sorting four integer labels on each neighboring qubit pair. 𝖲𝗈𝗋𝗍𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆𝗎𝗍𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{SortPermutation} (Algorithm 7) records the swaps that sort π\pi to the identity. Note that the final protocol 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖬𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁𝗀𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆𝗎𝗍𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{CompileMatchgatePermutation} (Algorithm 5) reverses this list before compiling it, which is necessary to implement the desired permutation π\pi (rather than π−1\pi^{-1}).

For an array a=(a1,…,a2​n)a=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{2n}), the qubit pair (j,j+1)(j,j+1) contains the four positions 2​j−1,2​j,2​j+1,2​j+22j-1,2j,2j+1,2j+2. We alternate the disjoint pairs

(2,3),(4,5),…;(1,2),(3,4),…(2,3),(4,5),\ldots;\qquad(1,2),(3,4),\ldots (S5.11)

which is a block version of odd–even transposition sorting 23. This framework was introduced previously for compiling continuous matchgate circuits 78; our version simplifies it by assuming the input is a matchgate permutation. Rather than block eliminations used there (a four-dimensional generalization of Givens rotations eliminations), each block of size-four permutations is locally sorted to yield a minimally sized sequence of nearest-neighboring Majorana swaps. This local operation 𝖲𝗈𝗋𝗍𝖥𝗈𝗎𝗋\mathsf{SortFour} is described in Algorithm 8.

Lemma S5.6 (Cost of a local four-label sort).

Algorithm 8 sorts its input with at most three swaps, at most two of which couple two qubits. Its swap count is at most the inversion number of its input, and its reversed swap list can be implemented with at most two CZ\mathrm{CZ} gates.

Proof.

The correctness of sorting is standard: at the start of the iteration for pp, all positions below pp already contain their target labels. If xp≠ypx_{p}\neq y_{p}, the destination qq of xpx_{p} therefore satisfies q>pq>p. Exchanging positions p,qp,q puts the label xpx_{p} in its final position qq. This leaves every previously fixed position unchanged, and so repeating this step eventually puts ypy_{p} at pp and hence sorts the block.

To count the swaps, we replace the four labels by their ranks 1,2,3,41,2,3,4. At a fixed pp, the while loop follows the cycle containing pp and removes one position from that cycle at each swap. A cycle of length ℓ\ell therefore gives ℓ−1\ell-1 swaps, all involving its smallest position pp. This is the standard minimal transposition factorization; if the local permutation has cc cycles, including fixed points, then the total is 4−c≤34-c\leq 3 (Sec. 26.13) 52. Sorting by adjacent inversions is another transposition factorization, with exactly inv⁡(x)\inv(x) swaps, so we have 4−c≤inv⁡(x)4-c\leq\inv(x).

Only a four-cycle requires three swaps: it uses the smallest position as its common endpoint and exchanges it once with each of the other three positions. Exactly one of those positions is on the same qubit, and the other two are on the neighboring qubit. Meanwhile, every other cycle type requires at most two swaps in total. The CZ\mathrm{CZ} bound therefore follows from Lemma S5.3. ∎

Compiling the swap list.

After 𝖲𝗈𝗋𝗍𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆𝗎𝗍𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{SortPermutation} (Algorithm 7), we reverse the list ℒ\mathscr{L} to bring it to the correct order for the quantum circuit. Then Algorithm 9 below compiles it into CZ\mathrm{CZ} and single-qubit Clifford gates. It assumes input pairs satisfy p<qp<q by convention and lie within one two-qubit local block. For a two-qubit pair, write the entry of Eq. S5.8 as Pp​q=ϵ​Aj​Bj+1P_{pq}=\epsilon A_{j}B_{j+1}, where ϵ∈{±1}\epsilon\in\{\pm 1\} and A,B∈{X,Y}A,B\in\{X,Y\}. Let HH denote the Hadamard gate, and write

CX=H,CY=S​H,CA​Z​CA†=A.C_{X}=H,\qquad C_{Y}=SH,\qquad C_{A}ZC_{A}^{\dagger}=A. (S5.12)

The following explicit form combines the local basis changes with the phase gates:

e−iϵπA⊗B/4=e−iϵπ/4(CASϵ⊗CBSϵ)CZ(CA†⊗CB†).e^{-i\epsilon\pi A\otimes B/4}=e^{-i\epsilon\pi/4}(C_{A}S^{\epsilon}\otimes C_{B}S^{\epsilon})\mathrm{CZ}(C_{A}^{\dagger}\otimes C_{B}^{\dagger}). (S5.13)

Thus, each such swap has two single-qubit Clifford gates before the CZ\mathrm{CZ} and two after it. We suppress all global phases throughout, although they can in principle be tracked if desired (e.g., for different applications that involve the controlled circuit).

Algorithm 9 produces a sign vector ss from the swap list, describing the circuit’s actual action Q=Ds​PπQ=D_{s}P_{\pi}. Thus, even if one begins with an unsigned permutation as input (as we do in Algorithm 5), we obtain a sign vector to track. In particular,

U†​Zj​U=s2​j−1​s2​j​(−i​γπ⁡(2​j−1)​γπ⁡(2​j)).U^{\dagger}Z_{j}U=s_{2j-1}s_{2j}\mathopen{}\left(-i\gamma_{\pi(2j-1)}\gamma_{\pi(2j)}\right)\mathclose{}. (S5.14)

Correctness and resource bounds.

We now prove the correctness of Algorithm 5 and establish the final circuit size.

Proof (of Theorem S5.1).

Write the sorting list as ℒ=((a1,b1),…,(am,bm))\mathscr{L}=((a_{1},b_{1}),\ldots,(a_{m},b_{m})) and put Tk=Tak​bkT_{k}=T_{a_{k}b_{k}}. Each swap exchanges two rows of PπP_{\pi}, and the sorted array represents the identity. Thus

Tm⋯T1Pπ=𝕀,Pπ=T1⋯Tm.T_{m}\cdots T_{1}P_{\pi}=\mathbb{I},\qquad P_{\pi}=T_{1}\cdots T_{m}. (S5.15)

Reading ℒ\mathscr{L} backward sets each (pk,qk)=(am+1−k,bm+1−k)(p_{k},q_{k})=(a_{m+1-k},b_{m+1-k}) in Eq. S5.1 and produces the desired permutation. Lemmas S5.3 and S5.4 and Algorithm 9 give a circuit UU implementing Ds​PπD_{s}P_{\pi}, with exactly the signs returned by the algorithm. Proposition S5.5 shows that its measurement basis agrees with that specified by π0\pi_{0}.

To bound the number of swaps, recall the standard inversion count:

inv⁡(a)=|{(p,q):p⁡<q,ap>​aq}|.\inv(a)=|\{(p,q):p<q,\ a_{p}>a_{q}\}|.

Completely sorting a contiguous four-label block decreases the global inversion count by exactly the inversion count of that block before sorting (Lemma S5.6). This removes its internal inversions, while its multiset of labels, and hence all inversions with positions outside the block, are unchanged. By the same lemma, the number of swaps this block incurs is at most this decrease. There are no inversions within an ordered pair, and since 𝖱𝖾𝖽𝗎𝖼𝖾𝖯𝖺𝗂𝗋𝗌\mathsf{ReducePairs} already ordered pairs by their first entries, each unordered pair of matched pairs contributes at most two inversions. Thus we have

m≤inv⁡(π)≤2​(n2)=n⁡(n−1).m\leq\inv(\pi)\leq 2\binom{n}{2}=n(n-1). (S5.16)

To bound the depth, first observe that Algorithm 7 sorts any permutation within at most nn sweeps of the four-Majorana blocks. Indeed, this is nothing but the well-known odd–even sort 23, regarding each block of four labels as a pair of pairs. This also implies that the classical work is 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}), dominated by sorting sweeps. By Lemma S5.6, each block requires two CZ\mathrm{CZ} gates, implying a depth of at most 2​n2n. All other gates within a block are single-qubit Cliffords, which we can merge to yield the structure

Mblock=(C1⊗C2)​CZ​(C3⊗C4)​CZ​(C5⊗C6).M_{\mathrm{block}}=(C_{1}\otimes C_{2})\mathrm{CZ}(C_{3}\otimes C_{4})\mathrm{CZ}(C_{5}\otimes C_{6}). (S5.17)

The last single-qubit layer of one sweep merges with the first of the next, implying a single-qubit depth bound of at most 2​n+12n+1.

For a uniform input π0\pi_{0}, the reduced matching is uniform 54, 25. Choose two of its matched pairs uniformly and condition on their four endpoints a<b<c<da<b<c<d. The three possible pairings

{{a,b},{c,d}},{{a,c},{b,d}},{{a,d},{b,c}}\{\{a,b\},\{c,d\}\},\qquad\{\{a,c\},\{b,d\}\},\qquad\{\{a,d\},\{b,c\}\} (S5.18)

are equally likely. After 𝖱𝖾𝖽𝗎𝖼𝖾𝖯𝖺𝗂𝗋𝗌\mathsf{ReducePairs}, they contribute respectively 00, 11, and 22 inversions. There are no inversions within an ordered pair, so summing over the (n2)\binom{n}{2} unordered pairs of matched pairs gives

𝔼[inv⁡(π)]=(n2)​0+1+23=n⁡(n−1)2,\E[\inv(\pi)]=\binom{n}{2}\frac{0+1+2}{3}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}, (S5.19)

recovering the expectation used in ref. 25. Each two-qubit Majorana swap requires one CZ\mathrm{CZ}, while each single-qubit swap requires none. Hence NCZ≤m≤inv⁡(π)N_{\mathrm{CZ}}\leq m\leq\inv(\pi), proving Eq. S5.3.

It is well known that the odd–even sort yields an 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n)-depth swap network 23; our blocked version expands each nearest neighbor into 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1)-sized blocks, so that argument also applies to our scheme. We only use 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) classical work, dominated by the cost of sorting length-𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) lists. This proves all claims. ∎

Comparison to optimal Haar-random constructions.

The work of Braccia et al. 8 provides a gate- and depth-optimal template for random matchgate circuits; this is advantageous over prior designs by fixing the circuit template (only needing to adjust rotation angles) and requiring 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) classical effort to generate a random instance, rather than previous 𝒪⁡(n3)\mathcal{O}(n^{3})-time algorithms. We opted for our new construction instead, which we observed yields smaller circuit sizes while still requiring only quadratic classical cost. We attribute this observation to a few properties:

  • •

    While they prove optimality for continuous matchgates, the authors explicitly acknowledge that the depth of the Clifford matchgate template is not optimal 8. Specifically, they use a triangular structure which has total and two-qubit depth at most 6​n−76n-7 and 4​n−64n-6, respectively (see their Lemma 3). Our design uses a more parallelized structure, achieving total and two-qubit depth bounds of 4​n+14n+1 and 2​n2n, respectively.

  • •

    Optimality of their fixed template is in expectation over the uniform measure; each specific instance may have a shorter-depth realization, which is what our construction targets. This is significant when implementing on noisy quantum hardware.

  • •

    They prove that the expected number of two-qubit gates in their design is 12​n​(n−12)\frac{1}{2}n(n-\frac{1}{2}) and essentially optimal, which is nearly identical to our Eq. S5.3.

S5.2 Use of spin-blocked matchgate shadows

We use spin-blocked matchgate shadows as introduced by Zhao and Miyake 78. This nearly halves the circuit depth and gate count, since they scale linearly and quadratically with the effective system size, respectively. This applies to the walker overlaps that we calculate in our chemistry experiments, since the associated Slater determinants factorize into α\alpha and β\beta spin sectors. In Fig. S1.3 we show a compiled example for 40 qubits: the α\alpha register (qubits 0–19) and the β\beta register (qubits 20–39) are acted on by independent random circuits, with no two-qubit gate between them. Due to the smaller effective system size and shallower depth, these circuits admit faster classical postprocessing (n→n/2n\to n/2), as well as experimentally lower overlap error measured from the noisy hardware (Fig. S3.4).

We do not introduce new theoretical results in this section, as we already carried out the spin-blocked analysis in previous work 78. Rather, here we review and clarify the theory and validity of spin-blocked shadows for the overlap estimation problem.

Formalism.

Let nα,nβn_{\alpha},n_{\beta} and ηα,ηβ\eta_{\alpha},\eta_{\beta} be the number of orbitals and electrons per spin, respectively. Order all α\alpha modes before all β\beta modes. A spin-blocked matchgate transformation is block diagonal,

Q=(Qα00Qβ)∈O⁡(2​nα)⊕O⁡(2​nβ),Q=\begin{pmatrix}Q_{\alpha}&0\\ 0&Q_{\beta}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathrm{O}(2n_{\alpha})\oplus\mathrm{O}(2n_{\beta}), (S5.20)

and a Slater matrix has the form

A=(Aα00Aβ),Aσ∈ℂησ×nσ,A=\begin{pmatrix}A_{\alpha}&0\\ 0&A_{\beta}\end{pmatrix},\qquad A_{\sigma}\in\mathbb{C}^{\eta_{\sigma}\times n_{\sigma}}, (S5.21)

with orthonormal rows. With occupied α\alpha rows placed before occupied β\beta rows, its creation operators give

|φ⟩=(∏j=1ηαdα,j†)​(∏k=1ηβdβ,k†)​|𝟎⟩=|φα⟩⊗|φβ⟩,dσ,j†=∑k=1nσ(Aσ)j​k∗​ak†.|\varphi\rangle=\left(\prod_{j=1}^{\eta_{\alpha}}d_{\alpha,j}^{\dagger}\right)\left(\prod_{k=1}^{\eta_{\beta}}d_{\beta,k}^{\dagger}\right)|\mathbf{0}\rangle=|\varphi_{\alpha}\rangle\otimes|\varphi_{\beta}\rangle,\qquad d_{\sigma,j}^{\dagger}=\sum_{k=1}^{n_{\sigma}}(A_{\sigma})_{jk}^{*}a_{k}^{\dagger}. (S5.22)

The vacuum also factorizes, so

|φ⟩​⟨𝟎|=|φα⟩​⟨𝟎α|⊗|φβ⟩​⟨𝟎β|.|\varphi\rangle\!\langle\mathbf{0}|=|\varphi_{\alpha}\rangle\!\langle\mathbf{0}_{\alpha}|\otimes|\varphi_{\beta}\rangle\!\langle\mathbf{0}_{\beta}|. (S5.23)

For even ηα,ηβ\eta_{\alpha},\eta_{\beta}, both factors lie in the even operator subspace Γeven,σ\Gamma_{\mathrm{even},\sigma} and hence are in the image of each spin sector’s shadow measurement channel

ℳα,β=ℳα⊗ℳβ.\mathcal{M}_{\alpha,\beta}=\mathcal{M}_{\alpha}\otimes\mathcal{M}_{\beta}. (S5.24)

Let ϱα​(Qα,bα)⊗ϱβ​(Qβ,bβ)\varrho_{\alpha}(Q_{\alpha},b_{\alpha})\otimes\varrho_{\beta}(Q_{\beta},b_{\beta}) be an i.i.d. spin-blocked snapshot of |𝟎⟩+|ΨT⟩2\frac{|\mathbf{0}\rangle+|\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}. The inverse on the joint outcome yields

2​tr⁡[|φ⟩​⟨𝟎|​(ℳα−1⊗ℳβ−1)​(Sα⊗Sβ)]=Xα​Xβ2,Xσ=2​tr⁡[|φσ⟩​⟨𝟎σ|​ℳσ−1​(ϱσ​(Qσ,bσ))].2\tr\mathopen{}\left[|\varphi\rangle\!\langle\mathbf{0}|(\mathcal{M}_{\alpha}^{-1}\otimes\mathcal{M}_{\beta}^{-1})(S_{\alpha}\otimes S_{\beta})\right]\mathclose{}=\frac{X_{\alpha}X_{\beta}}{2},\qquad X_{\sigma}=2\tr\mathopen{}\left[|\varphi_{\sigma}\rangle\!\langle\mathbf{0}_{\sigma}|\mathcal{M}_{\sigma}^{-1}(\varrho_{\sigma}(Q_{\sigma},b_{\sigma}))\right]\mathclose{}. (S5.25)

Thus 𝔼[Xα​Xβ/2]=⟨ΨT|φ⟩\E\mathopen{}\left[X_{\alpha}X_{\beta}/2\right]\mathclose{}=\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}|\varphi\rangle. Importantly, this does not require any symmetry of the quantum state, although each ησ\eta_{\sigma} must be even (as is the case with standard matchgate shadow overlaps). We can handle odd electron numbers by appending a dummy occupied orbital to the trial state, e.g., |ΨT⟩→|1⟩α​|1⟩β​|ΨT⟩|\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}\rangle\to|1\rangle_{\alpha}|1\rangle_{\beta}|\Psi_{\mathrm{T}}\rangle. The Slater coefficient matrices must also be extended via

Aσ′=(100Aσ)A_{\sigma}^{\prime}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&A_{\sigma}\end{pmatrix} (S5.26)

Finally, we can apply the same polynomial subroutines from Section S4 separately to the two spin blocks without any modification. The classical computational cost therefore improves from 𝒪⁡((nα+nβ)3)\mathcal{O}((n_{\alpha}+n_{\beta})^{3}) to 𝒪⁡(nα3+nβ3)\mathcal{O}(n_{\alpha}^{3}+n_{\beta}^{3}).
